title: CodeHealth Outperforms Perplexity as LLM Refactoring Safety Predictor
summary: A Jan 2026 arXiv paper (Borg et al., 2601.02200) studied 5,000 Python files and found a meaningful correlation between human-calibrated code health metrics and semantic preservation after AI refactoring. CodeHealth (CH) outperforms both perplexity and SLOC as predictors of LLM refactoring correctness, with risk reduction of 15-30% on high-health code. The practical implication: code health scoring already captures AI-readiness without needing a separate 'perplexity' biomarker. This validates the project's approach (human-friendly = AI-friendly), while also suggesting that the score should be surfaced as a per-file 'AI refactoring risk' rating: high CH = low risk = good candidate for automated fix, low CH = manual-first. The paper also shows that well-factored modular code reduces LLM hallucination risk.
evidence: CodeHealth outperforms perplexity (LLM-intrinsic confidence metric) and SLOC as predictor of refactoring correctness; 15-30% risk reduction on high-CH code across 5,000-file dataset. Published Jan 2026.

title: AI-Generated Code Has Distinct Smell Fingerprints: New Biomarkers Needed
summary: Two 2025-2026 papers (arXiv 2605.02741 and 2510.03029) characterize LLM-generated code smell patterns. Key finding: 52-78% of LLM-generated code contains at least one smell despite 98.5% syntactic validity. LLMs produce procedural smells (Long Method, Temporal Field) at higher rates than human authors; human authors produce more state-management smells. Three AI-specific patterns emerge that could be new biomarkers: (1) 'Reasoning-Complexity Paradox' — capable models generate procedural bloat in single methods (measurable as function length vs. cyclomatic complexity ratio), (2) 'Modular Mirage' — superficial file separation without semantic cohesion (measurable as Scattered Functionality / low cohesion in short files), (3) 'God Class Syndrome' in manager files. Volume-Quality Inverse Law: near-perfect correlation (rho=0.94) between code volume and architectural degradation in LLM agents. The Propensity Smelly Score (PSC) metric is proposed for benchmarking LLMs. The project's existing smells (GodClass, BrainMethod, ComplexMethod) cover the most common LLM-induced smells but miss Temporal Field (class-level variable used by only a subset of methods) and Scattered Functionality.
evidence: 52-78% of LLM-generated code contains at least one smell; rho=0.94 correlation between code volume and architectural degradation in agent-driven dev. Temporal Field and Scattered Functionality are confirmed missing from project's 28 biomarkers.

title: Architectural Smell Tier is Missing: 7 Types Beyond Class-Level Smells
summary: SmellBench (arXiv 2605.07001, May 2026) introduces a multi-dimensional scoring approach for architectural smell repair. PyExamine identifies 7 architectural smell types not currently in the project's 28 biomarkers: Hub-like Dependency (excessive incoming dependencies to a module), Scattered Functionality (related behaviors fragmented cross-module), Cyclic Dependency (circular module deps), Unstable Dependency (deps on volatile modules), Improper API Usage (repetitive incorrect API invocations), and Redundant Abstractions (duplicate implementations). Key finding: 63.1% of detected architectural smells are false positives — this is critical for the project's scoring formula, as false positives inflate score penalties unfairly. The best LLM agent achieves only 47.7% resolution on architectural smells vs. the project's reported 20% mechanical fix rate and 9.5-reachability in 2-6 iterations for code-level smells. Architectural smells require cross-module reasoning that LLMs lack. ROSE (arXiv 2507.12561) uses CodeBERT/CodeT5 fine-tuned on 2M refactoring instances for architectural smell recommendations with 97% accuracy / 95% F1.
evidence: 7 architectural smell types identified by PyExamine; 63.1% false positive rate from automated detection tools; best LLM repair agent reaches only 47.7% resolution on architectural smells. Cyclic dependency and hub-like dependency absent from project's current biomarker set.

title: Evolutionary + Structural Metric Fusion Significantly Improves Smell Prediction
summary: A 2025 ScienceDirect paper proposes fusing evolutionary metrics (change frequency per version, number of committers, age of code, co-change patterns) with structural metrics for design smell prediction, finding that combined metrics outperform structural-only across all smell types. The project already has temporal/behavioral analytics (hotspots, churn, bus factor, knowledge loss) and MethodTemporalCoupling. However, the research shows that per-class or per-function evolution metrics (not just file-level) applied to smell detection thresholds — especially for GodClass and FeatureEnvy — markedly improve precision. Specifically, frequently modified classes that also have high complexity are far more reliably flagged as god classes than infrequently modified complex ones. This suggests the project could weight its existing smell penalties by churn rate: smells in frequently-modified files (hotspots) should carry higher weight as they cause more actual defect risk.
evidence: Combined evolutionary+structural metrics outperform structural-only for all design smell types in 2025 multi-version Java study. The project has churn data but does not currently apply it as a weight modifier to individual smell penalties.

title: Exception Handling Anti-Patterns: A Largely Absent Biomarker Class
summary: Validated research (IEEE ICPC 2017; updated 2026 study) finds 5 exception handling anti-patterns prevalent in >20% of catch blocks: Unhandled Exceptions (40.8%), Catch Generic (31.9%), Unreachable Handler (28.0%), Over-catch (24.6%), Destructive Wrapping (22.3%). A 2026 study found >70% violations for Catch Generic alone. These are not currently in the project's 28 biomarkers beyond possibly overlapping with 'DeadCode'. These patterns are straightforwardly detectable via AST traversal: empty catch bodies, catch(Exception e), unreachable handlers after broader catches, re-throwing as RuntimeException losing stack trace. All Tier A languages (TypeScript, Java, Python, Go, etc.) can detect these via tree-sitter AST. Exception smells directly correlate with reliability defects, not just maintainability, giving them high defect-prediction value. Adding 3-5 exception smell sub-types as a new biomarker group would fill a meaningful gap.
evidence: Catch Generic found in 31.9% of catch blocks; 2026 study finds >70% violation rate. Five anti-patterns confirmed in >20% of catch blocks across 16 Java/C# projects. Not in project's current 28 biomarkers.

title: Promise/Async Anti-Patterns: TypeScript/JavaScript-Specific Missing Biomarker
summary: DrAsync (ICSE 2022, IEEE) identified 8 async anti-patterns in JavaScript, finding 2,600+ static instances across 20 popular repos. Key detectable patterns via static AST: (1) async functions with no await (unnecessary promise allocation), (2) redundant await on return (awaiting what's already a promise), (3) missing return in .then() handlers breaking promise chains, (4) unnecessary sequential awaits on independent operations (parallelization opportunity), (5) unhandled promise rejections. These are directly detectable in the TypeScript/JavaScript Tier A tree-sitter grammar today with no additional dependencies. The project's current smells don't include async-specific patterns, yet these are among the most common real-world JS/TS bugs and hurt both correctness and performance. Adding even 2-3 of these as TypeScript/JS-specific biomarkers would be highly differentiated vs SonarQube (which only covers subset).
evidence: 2,600+ static anti-pattern instances found in 20 popular JS repos. 8 specific anti-pattern types with static-analysis detection methods published. TypeScript/JS are Tier A in project; tree-sitter can detect these patterns without additional parsers.

title: Test Smell Detection as a Distinct Biomarker Class (22 Named Types)
summary: 2025 research (Springer Empirical Software Engineering, arXiv 2410.10628) confirms LLM-generated test code carries disproportionately high test smell rates. The taxonomy includes: Assertion Roulette (multiple assertions without messages), Duplicate Assert, Conditional Logic in tests, Sleepy Test (hard-coded waits), Empty Test, Useless Test, Mystery Guest (undeclared external resources), Magic Number Test, General Fixture. Assertion Roulette and Sleepy Test best predict flaky tests. LLMs produce these at higher rates than human-written tests. Multi-agent approaches achieve 96% detection (pass@5) and 75% automated refactoring for classic smells. Test smells are absent from the project's 28 biomarkers. Adding a TestSmell biomarker group for Tier A languages (with existing test-file detection) could differentiate the product and address a growing pain point as AI-generated tests proliferate. Detection requires identifying test files (jest/pytest patterns) and checking assertion and control flow AST nodes.
evidence: 22+ named test smells in taxonomy; Assertion Roulette most common in both open-source and industrial code; LLM-generated test smells studied empirically in 2025. Not in project's 28 biomarkers.

title: Context-Specific Metric Threshold Calibration via Logistic Regression on Fault Data
summary: A 2026 arXiv paper (2602.06831) proposes ROC-curve-based threshold derivation from fault-prone function data as superior to universal percentile methods (Alves approach). The project already uses empirical calibration for Java (Defects4J), but the paper demonstrates that: (1) context-specific thresholds outperform universal ones, (2) logistic regression + ROC achieves comparable performance to supervised ML while being more transparent/explainable, (3) the approach is validated in safety-critical automotive firmware. Key practical implication: the project's AI_READY=9.5 and HEALTHY=9.0 thresholds are empirically calibrated only for Java. Per-language calibration for Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust using language-specific open defect datasets (bugs.python.org, GitHub issue tracker with labels) could significantly improve the score's reliability for non-Java languages. The Alves approach used for other languages produces thresholds not validated against fault data.
evidence: ROC curve method outperforms Alves Rankings for fault prediction; project confirms calibration only for Java (Defects4J); 24 metrics studied in automotive firmware showing stable cross-dataset thresholds.

title: Identifier Naming Quality: LLMs Most Sensitive Metric, Currently Underweighted
summary: A July 2025 arXiv paper (2507.05289) measured LLM code quality evaluation sensitivity to readability attributes. Key finding: confusing identifier names caused score reductions of 3.1% to 78.9% across 9 LLMs, far larger than comment removal effects. 'Poor Variable/Method Names' mentions jumped from 4 to 890 in evaluations when names were obfuscated. All 9 LLMs showed 100% agreement that naming was the most impactful readability factor. The project's existing NamingClarity biomarker captures some of this, but the research confirms naming quality should likely carry a higher weight than currently assigned — it is the single biggest readability signal both for humans and LLMs. Additionally, specific naming anti-patterns detectable via static analysis (single-letter variables outside loops, doppelganger names differing by one char, abbreviations under 4 chars in public APIs) are not currently enumerated as sub-categories. IDEAL tool (arXiv 2107.08344) provides an open-source implementation.
evidence: Score reductions 3.1-78.9% from naming obfuscation across 9 LLMs; 'Poor Variable/Method Names' mentions 4→890 when names confusing. Project has NamingClarity but does not detect sub-patterns like single-letter variables, doppelgangers, or abbreviation anti-patterns.

title: Code Clone Rate is Rising 4x Under AI Assistance — Duplicate Code Needs Semantic Detection
summary: GitClear's 2025 analysis of 211M changed lines of code (Google, Microsoft, Meta repos) found AI-assisted development drove code clone rates from 8.3% (2021) to 12.3% (2024) — approximately 4x growth. Refactoring rates collapsed from 25% to <10% of changed lines. This makes duplicate/cloned code detection a critical biomarker for the AI era. The project's current biomarkers don't appear to include a dedicated DuplicateCode/CodeClone smell. Type 1-3 clones (textual/token similarity) are detectable statically; Type 4 (semantic) require embedding models. For the project's MCP use case, adding a lightweight Type 1-3 clone detector (token comparison within and across files, configurable threshold e.g. 6+ identical lines) would be immediately actionable and directly addresses the AI-era code quality degradation pattern. The metric would incentivize AI loops to consolidate rather than duplicate.
evidence: Clone rate 8.3%→12.3% (2021-2024) in 211M lines; refactoring rate 25%→<10%. No dedicated DuplicateCode biomarker in project's current 28 smells. Directly measurable via token comparison within tree-sitter AST.

title: CodeScene is the closest direct competitor — same 1–10 score, same self-correcting loop concept, now MCP-native
summary: CodeScene's CodeHealth MCP server (€8–9/month) exposes code_health_review, pre_commit_code_health_safeguard, and delta review tools. It runs fully locally, claims 90–100% AI fix rates with MCP guidance vs ~20% without, and uses a 1–10 score (9.5+ = AI-ready). Their whitepaper (Jan 2026, peer-reviewed) quantifies that AI assistants increase defect risk 30–60% on unhealthy code (score <7). A public Java-only benchmark (70 human experts, 500 files, 9 projects) shows CodeScene F-score 83% vs SonarQube 13.3% — but this was self-published by founder Adam Tornhill and is Java-only (Schnappinger et al. dataset). Their MCP server is open source (codescene-oss/codescene-mcp-server on GitHub) with pre-built AGENTS.md agent skills. Key weakness: requires a paid CodeScene subscription (access token) for project-level features like hotspots, goals, and ownership; local-only token gives scoring/review but no git history integration.
evidence: CodeScene MCP page: '90–100% fix rate with MCP-augmented CodeHealth data vs ~20% baseline'; Whitepaper: 'AI increases defect risk by at least 30% on unhealthy code'; F-score study: 83% vs 13.3% on Schnappinger dataset. Source: codescene.com/blog/6x-improvement-over-sonarqube

title: SonarQube now has an MCP server — but it is cloud-dependent, requires Docker, and has no 1–10 health score
summary: SonarSource released an official MCP server (2025) that exposes quality gate status, issue queries, security hotspot lookups, SCA dependency risks, and a new 'Sonar way for agentic AI' quality profile (Java, JS/TS, Python). It runs as a Docker container pointed at a SonarQube instance (cloud or server). Critical limitations: (1) heavy analysis tools disabled in SonarQube Cloud to protect shared infrastructure; (2) Context Augmentation tools require local filesystem mount unavailable in hosted mode; (3) dependency risk tools require SonarQube Server 2025.4 Enterprise or higher; (4) SonarQube scores A–E grades, not a numeric 1–10 health scale — no structured delta instruction output. Their scoring is rule-count-based (maintainability rating by remediation time), not weighted-smell aggregation. The 6x F-score gap vs CodeScene indicates their scoring poorly correlates with actual maintainability.
evidence: SonarQube MCP docs: 'Heavy analysis tools are disabled to protect the shared SonarQube Cloud infrastructure'; 'Context Augmentation tools are not available because they require a local filesystem mount'; 'Dependency risks are only available when connecting to SonarQube Server 2025.4 Enterprise or higher with Advanced Security enabled'. Source: docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-mcp-server

title: act101 — the most capable automated AST transformer competitor: 163 languages, 183 refactor operations via MCP
summary: act101 (act101.ai) is a Rust binary MCP server exposing 183 AST-aware refactor operations across 163 language grammars including extract-function, rename, move-symbol, convert-to-dataclass, extract-trait, inline, add-type-hints, generate-init, organize-imports. It includes 30 codebase analyzers: cohesion, coupling, cycles, chokepoints, hotspots, dead code, layers, seams, clusters, surface, fan balance, migration readiness, type completeness. Pricing: Free (personal, 15 queries, 3 analyzers), Pro $19/month (10 analyzers, extract/inline), Teams $39/seat/month (deep structural ops), Elite $99/seat/month (25 premium languages: COBOL, Fortran, Ada, Verilog, Solidity). This directly fills the gap where Healthy AI Code MCP only has automated transformers for TS/JS/PHP. The key differentiator vs Healthy AI Code MCP: act101 does transformation without health scoring; Healthy AI Code MCP scores and instructs but relies on the LLM for most transformations. A partnership or integration could be mutually beneficial.
evidence: act101.ai: '163 grammars, 183 AST refactor operations, 30 codebase analyzers, 8 porting operations — exposed to Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and OpenCode through a built-in MCP server.' Pricing tiers confirmed from WebFetch of act101.ai.

title: Qodo (formerly CodiumAI) raised $70M Series B for multi-agent code review — no numeric health score, focuses on PR verification
summary: Qodo 2.0 (Feb 2026) introduced multi-agent code review architecture and a RAG-powered 'Qodo Aware' context engine indexing entire codebases cross-repo. Qodo ranked #1 on Martian's Code Review Bench at 64.3% — 10+ points above competitors, 25 points above Claude Code Review. However, Qodo does not expose a numeric code health score or a self-correcting refactoring loop; it is PR-level review, not file-level biomarker analysis. Their moat is context depth (cross-repo RAG) and test generation. The gap Healthy AI Code MCP exploits: Qodo reviews PR diffs but does not compute a continuous, git-history-aware health score per file that an agent can target. Qodo's $70M war chest means they will likely expand into health scoring territory.
evidence: Search results: 'Qodo raised $70M Series B...explicitly positioning itself against software slop'; 'Qodo ranked No. 1 on Martian's Code Review Bench with a score of 64.3% — more than 10 points ahead of the nearest competitor.' Source: effloow.com/articles/best-ai-code-review-tools-coderabbit-claude-qodo-2026

title: DeepSource's Report Card (A–D across 5 dimensions) and <5% false positive rate are key messaging differentiators
summary: DeepSource uses a graded Report Card (A–D) across Security, Reliability, Complexity, Hygiene, and Coverage — distinct from the 1–10 numeric scale. Their claim of <5% false positive rate is a core marketing differentiator vs SonarQube (which has high false positive rates, especially for complex rules). DeepSource's Autofix feature uses AI to generate and apply fixes for detected issues. The five-dimension framing (vs a single aggregate score) resonates with teams that want granular attribution. Healthy AI Code MCP's single aggregate score is simpler for agent targeting but harder to explain to engineering managers who want dimension breakdowns. Recommendation: expose per-dimension subscores (security, complexity, maintainability) alongside the aggregate 1–10 score.
evidence: Search results: 'DeepSource's Report Card system — a graded assessment (A through D) across five dimensions: Security, Reliability, Complexity, Hygiene, and Coverage... claims a false positive rate under 5%, significantly lower than most static analysis tools.' Source: deepsource.com

title: tree-sitter-analyzer (open-source MIT) exposes 62 MCP tools with TOON format achieving 50–70% token savings — direct structural overlap
summary: tree-sitter-analyzer (github.com/aimasteracc/tree-sitter-analyzer) is a free MIT-licensed local MCP server providing 62 tools including check_project_health, check_file_health, safe_to_edit, modification_guard, codegraph_complexity_heatmap, codegraph_dead_code, codegraph_similarity, and symbol_lineage. Full AST indexing covers 13 languages (Python, Java, JS, TS, Go, Rust, C, C++, C#, Swift, Kotlin, Ruby, PHP). Its TOON (tabular JSON) output format reduces token payloads by 50–70% vs raw JSON. Benchmark: −11% median cost vs CodeGraph's −4% across 6 repos. It is free and open-source vs Healthy AI Code MCP's local-only (no subscription). Key gaps in tree-sitter-analyzer: no weighted health score (1–10), no biomarker taxonomy, no self-correcting loop tooling, no MethodTemporalCoupling, no security smell detection. Healthy AI Code MCP's quantitative scoring and 28-biomarker taxonomy remain its structural advantage.
evidence: WebFetch of github.com/aimasteracc/tree-sitter-analyzer: 'TOON achieves token efficiency through a tabular JSON variant that cuts payload by ~50-70% vs raw JSON'; '13 languages with full indexing'; 'MIT-licensed open-source software'.

title: Codacy MCP server covers 40+ languages with Grade+Issues+Duplication+Complexity+Coverage per file — cloud-dependent
summary: The official Codacy MCP server (github.com/codacy/codacy-mcp-server) exposes codacy_get_file_with_analysis returning Grade, Issues, Duplication, Complexity, and Coverage metrics per file, plus codacy_cli_analyze for local runs, and SRM-based security tools. It supports 40+ languages. Critical difference: Codacy's analysis runs on cloud infrastructure (asynchronous, no CI/CD blocking) — so it cannot analyze uncommitted code in a local refactoring loop without codacy_cli_analyze. Codacy's grade is letter-based (not 1–10 numeric), making it less suitable as an agent's convergence target. Healthy AI Code MCP's synchronous, fully local, numeric score with delta predictions is more loop-friendly. Codacy's moat: coverage metrics and SRM security dashboard, which Healthy AI Code MCP does not currently surface.
evidence: Search results on Codacy MCP: 'codacy_get_file_with_analysis: Get detailed analysis information for a file, including metrics for Grade, Issues, Duplication, Complexity, and Coverage'; 'codacy_cli_analyze: Run quality analysis locally using Codacy CLI'. Source: github.com/codacy/codacy-mcp-server

title: Peer-reviewed research (Jan 2026) shows AI-friendly code metrics meaningfully predict LLM refactoring success across 5,000 Python files
summary: The arXiv paper 'Code for Machines, Not Just Humans: Quantifying AI-Friendliness with Code Health Metrics' (arXiv:2601.02200) validated CodeHealth as a predictor of LLM semantic preservation across 5,000 Python files from competitive programming. Finding: 'meaningful association between CodeHealth and semantic preservation when LLMs perform refactoring tasks' — human-friendly code is also more compatible with AI tooling. This supports Healthy AI Code MCP's core thesis and provides citable academic backing. However, the study uses only Python and competitive-programming code (potentially not representative of real enterprise codebases). Competitors like CodeScene are already citing this research in their sales materials. Healthy AI Code MCP could similarly cite this and pursue comparable validation for other languages.
evidence: arXiv:2601.02200 abstract: 'meaningful association between CodeHealth and semantic preservation when LLMs perform refactoring tasks... tested across 5,000 Python files from competitive programming contexts.' Published January 2026.

title: AI-specific code smells (22 ML smells, 95.8% precision) are an unaddressed biomarker category in current tool landscape
summary: arXiv:2509.20491 'AI-Specific Code Smells: From Specification to Detection' identifies 22 ML-specific code smells detectable with SpecDetect4ML using Code Property Graphs (CPGs), achieving 95.82% precision and 88.14% recall across 890 ML systems. These affect reproducibility, robustness, and maintainability (e.g., data leakage, silent failures). The existing landscape: CodeSmile implements 12 of 22, mlpylint implements 20. SonarQube, CodeScene, Codacy, DeepSource, and Healthy AI Code MCP currently have no dedicated ML-smell detection. With AI-generated code now comprising ~42% of committed code (SonarSource stat), ML/AI-specific smells are a rapidly growing category. Adding even a subset (e.g., data leakage patterns, missing reproducibility seeds, unsafe tensor operations) would differentiate Healthy AI Code MCP in the AI-native segment.
evidence: arXiv:2509.20491: 'SpecDetect4ML achieved 95.82% precision and 88.14% recall on a unified ground truth when evaluated across 890 machine learning systems'; '22 ML code smells specified'; 'patterns affecting reproducibility, robustness, and maintainability'.

title: Vibe coding creates 4x code duplication and ~50% security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code — undetected by most tools at commit time
summary: Multiple 2025-2026 sources document that 'vibe coding' workflows (prompt-generate-glance-commit, used by 85%+ of developers weekly) produce: ~50% of AI-generated code containing security vulnerabilities (primarily injection variants); up to 4x code duplication across sessions; architectural inconsistency because different AI sessions generate contradictory implementations. Healthy AI Code MCP already detects HardcodedCredential, SqlInjectionRisk, XssRisk, CommandInjectionRisk, and DeepNesting. The gap is cross-session duplication detection (clone smells across files) and a 'vibe-coding pattern' smell for AI-characteristic anti-patterns (e.g., missing error handling, hardcoded paths in build scripts per arXiv:2601.16839). A 'VibeCodingDebt' composite smell could surface these at commit time.
evidence: Search results: 'studies of AI-generated code consistently find that nearly half of all output contains security vulnerabilities'; 'code duplication increasing up to 4x'; 'AI-generated build code identified 364 maintainability and security-related build smells, such as lack of error handling and hardcoded paths' (arXiv:2601.16839).

title: MCP 2026-07-28 RC: Stateless Core Removes Session Overhead
summary: The 2026-07-28 MCP release candidate (locked May 21 2026, ships July 28) makes the protocol fully stateless. The initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-Id are eliminated; protocol version, client identity, and capabilities now travel in _meta on every JSON-RPC request. A new server/discover method replaces stateful capability negotiation. New response metadata fields ttlMs and cacheScope enable intelligent client-side caching. Headers Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name allow routing without body inspection. For this project, this means the server can run behind a plain round-robin load balancer — no sticky sessions, no shared session store. Tool-call results with ttlMs can be cached client-side, which is directly applicable to repeated code_health_review calls on the same unchanged file. The state-visible handle pattern lets models pass back opaque identifiers between calls rather than relying on server-side session memory.
evidence: RC blog: 'every request carries its own protocol version, client identity, and negotiated capabilities inside the _meta object'; ttlMs and cacheScope in response metadata for client-side caching; Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name headers for routing

title: outputSchema + structuredContent: Machine-Readable Tool Outputs Reduce Prompt Token Waste
summary: The MCP 2025-11-25 spec (and strengthened in 2026 RC) defines outputSchema as a JSON Schema on each tool definition. When present, the server MUST return results in a structuredContent field conforming to the schema; for backward compat it SHOULD also include a text serialization. The 2026 RC lifts the restriction that structuredContent be an object — any JSON value is valid, and full JSON Schema 2020-12 (oneOf, anyOf, allOf, $ref) is supported. This project's tools currently return free-text or loosely structured text blobs. Declaring outputSchema for tools like code_health_review (with typed fields: score, smells[], loopComplete, followUpInstruction) enables: (1) client-side validation so malformed responses fail fast; (2) LLM reasoning directly on the typed object without re-parsing text; (3) potential use of Anthropic's structured-outputs-2025-11-13 beta which caches tool schemas for 24h. The project already documents the structured-outputs beta header but does not yet expose outputSchema in its MCP tool definitions.
evidence: Spec: 'If an output schema is provided, Servers MUST provide structured results that conform to this schema. Clients SHOULD validate structured results against this schema.' 2026 RC: outputSchema unrestricted, structuredContent accepts any JSON value, full JSON Schema 2020-12 composition supported.

title: Tool Annotations Enable Auto-Approval of Read-Only Analysis Tools
summary: MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) are now a stable part of the spec. All code_health_* read-only tools (review, report, explain_smell, etc.) qualify for readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false, idempotentHint: true, openWorldHint: false. When a trusted MCP server sets these, supporting clients (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) can auto-approve invocations without confirmation dialogs. This eliminates the human-approval round-trip on every loop iteration. The code_health_auto_refactor and apply_auto_refactor tools, which do write files, should carry destructiveHint: true and idempotentHint: false. A Tool Annotations Interest Group (Microsoft, OpenAI, AWS, Cloudflare, Anthropic) is extending the vocabulary; future hints may address output sensitivity (relevant for credential detection results). Default values are worst-case (destructive, non-idempotent, open-world) — so adding correct annotations now immediately improves UX for loop-running clients.
evidence: Annotation blog: 'A tool marked readOnlyHint: true from a trusted server might be auto-approved, while destructiveHint: true gets a confirmation step.' Spec default is worst-case. Interest Group expanding vocabulary.

title: MCP Elicitation Enables Mid-Loop Structured Parameter Collection
summary: MCP elicitation (introduced 2025-11-25, Claude Code support shipped March 14 2026 v2.1.76) lets the server pause tool execution and request structured input from the user via a typed JSON Schema form. In the 2026 RC, persistent connections are not required — the server returns InputRequiredResult with the elicitation prompt, and any server instance processes the retry. Practical applications for this project: (1) code_health_set_goal can elicit target score and file path via a form rather than requiring the user to know the exact parameter schema; (2) code_health_auto_refactor can elicit confirmation of which smell to prioritize when multiple equal-weight smells exist; (3) first-run configuration (project root, language overrides) can be collected interactively. URL mode is required for anything sensitive (API keys, credentials). Form mode works for all preference/config inputs. This reduces friction for first-time users and non-developer AI operators.
evidence: Claude Code changelog: MCP Elicitation support added v2.1.76 March 14 2026. Spec: form mode for structured data collection, URL mode for sensitive data. 2026 RC: multi-round-trip via InputRequiredResult without persistent connections.

title: MCP Tasks Extension: Async Long-Running Analysis with Progress Streaming
summary: The Tasks primitive (introduced experimental in 2025-11-25, graduated to extension in 2026 RC) upgrades MCP from synchronous tool calls to call-now/fetch-later. A tool returns immediately with a durable handle; real work runs in the background; clients poll tasks/get or subscribe. Task management: tasks/get, tasks/result, tasks/list, tasks/cancel. Progress reuses MCP's existing progressToken mechanism. Applicable tools for this project: (1) analyzeFileWithHistory (which runs git log operations that can be slow on large repos) could return a task handle immediately and stream progress; (2) a new 'analyze_repository' tool that scans all files could run async; (3) code_health_refactoring_loop could become a long-running task with per-iteration progress events. The execution field on tool definitions now accepts taskSupport: 'forbidden' | 'optional' | 'required' — this is negotiated at the tool level. Adopting Tasks would allow running the full 2-6 iteration refactoring loop as a single async task rather than requiring the client to orchestrate each iteration.
evidence: Spec: taskSupport field in tool execution object (forbidden/optional/required). Tasks are augmentation to tools/call, sampling/createMessage, elicitation/create. Progress reuses progressToken. 2026 RC: Tasks graduates to extension, clients drive via tasks/get and tasks/update.

title: Dynamic Toolsets (Just-in-Time Tool Loading) Cuts Context Window Usage 90-96%
summary: Research (Speakeasy, 2025) demonstrates that replacing static tool lists with a search_tools + describe_tools pattern achieves 96.4% token reduction on simple tasks and 90.7% on complex tasks, with zero degradation in success rate. The mechanism: (1) expose a search_tools tool (semantic embedding search) plus a describe_tools tool (retrieve schema on demand); (2) the agent queries for relevant tools by category/keyword before deciding what to call; (3) full JSON schemas are loaded only for the tools actually used. For a 27-tool MCP server, static loading burns those 27 schemas on every context. Dynamic loading means the agent only sees schemas for the 2-3 tools it will actually call per loop iteration. Trade-off: ~50% increase in execution time from extra tool calls. The project already has 27 tools and CLAUDE.md notes the project documents token tips — but this specific pattern of exposing a search_tools meta-tool is not implemented. Implementation requires: (a) list_changed notification support for dynamic registration, (b) a search_tools meta-tool with embeddings or keyword matching, (c) a describe_tools tool that returns the full inputSchema/outputSchema for named tools.
evidence: Speakeasy benchmark: input tokens reduced 96.7% (simple) and 91.2% (complex); total tokens down 96.4%/90.7%; 100% success rate maintained; ~50% execution time increase. Mechanism: search_tools (semantic) + describe_tools (schema-on-demand) = 6-8 tool calls vs 3 in static.

title: Tool Description Quality: 97% of MCP Tools Have Descriptions with Detectable Smells
summary: A 2026 research paper (arXiv 2602.14878) audited MCP tool descriptions and found 97.1% contain at least one 'smell'. Six smell categories: unclear purpose (56% of tools), unstated limitations (~90%), missing usage guidelines, opaque parameters, underspecified descriptions, exemplar issues. Augmenting descriptions with all six components raises task success rate +5.85 percentage points and evaluator score +15.12%. However, average execution steps increase 67.46% (more LLM reasoning overhead). Ablation finding: dropping the Examples component did not significantly degrade performance — meaning the highest ROI additions are (1) explicit purpose statement, (2) guidelines (when to use/not use), (3) limitations, (4) detailed parameter explanations. For this project's 27 tools, the descriptions should be audited against these six dimensions. Particularly critical: code_health_review should state when NOT to use it (e.g., 'do not call this on generated files or minified code'), code_health_auto_refactor should document which languages support automated rewrites vs. smell-detection-only.
evidence: arXiv 2602.14878: 97.1% of tool descriptions have >=1 smell; augmented descriptions +5.85pp task success rate, +15.12% evaluator score; execution step increase 67.46%; removing Examples did not significantly degrade performance.

title: MCP Sampling: Server-Driven LLM Calls Enable Self-Contained Refactor Loop
summary: MCP sampling allows a server to request LLM completions from the client (sampling/createMessage) rather than requiring an external API call. This enables the server to run its own reasoning steps internally. For this project's refactoring loop, a server-side implementation using sampling could: (1) call code_health_review internally, (2) use sampling to ask the connected LLM 'given these smells, what refactor should I apply?', (3) apply the refactor, (4) re-review, and loop to completion — all within a single tool call from the client's perspective. Combined with the Tasks extension, this creates a fully server-orchestrated refactoring loop where the client fires one tool call and receives a completed refactor. The human-in-the-loop constraint is maintained because the client mediates all sampling requests (the user can deny any LLM call the server makes). This pattern is specifically designed for agentic use cases and self-correcting loops.
evidence: MCP sampling spec: server sends sampling/createMessage to client; client acts as intermediary between server, user, and model. Use case: server-side agent loops where AI planning asks 'what to do next?' and gets model response. Combined with Tasks: single async task handles entire multi-iteration loop.

title: MCP Registry Listing Strategy: Smithery + Official Registry for Maximum Discoverability
summary: The official MCP Registry (launched September 2025, at registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) serves as the canonical source of truth that client sub-registries and third-party marketplaces pull from. Smithery (>7,000 servers) is the primary destination for agent framework users. MCPMarket.com lists 10,000+ servers across 23+ categories. Key discoverability requirements: (1) server record must include name, transport type, tool list, auth requirement, homepage URL, and a capability description — records missing auth or transport info are skipped by automated filters; (2) Smithery offers UI-based config forms replacing manual env-var setup, which reduces installation friction; (3) semantic search-based discovery (embeddings of tool name, description, inputSchema) is used by advanced registries — so tool names and descriptions directly affect SEO-equivalent ranking. For this project, none of the current tools use the service-prefix pattern (should be healthy_ai_code_review, not code_health_review) and the server is not yet listed on Smithery or the official registry. These are high-leverage, low-effort distribution improvements.
evidence: Registry blog: 'standardizing how servers are distributed and discovered, expanding reach'; Smithery: 7,000+ servers, CLI install or hosted remote; MCPMarket: 10,000+ servers; records without auth/transport skipped by automated filters; semantic search uses embeddings of name+description+schema.

title: MCP Resource Subscriptions: Push-Based Notifications When Analyzed Files Change
summary: MCP resources support subscriptions (resources/subscribe + notifications/resources/updated). A client can subscribe to a specific file URI and receive a push notification when that file changes, triggering re-analysis without polling. This is directly applicable: after code_health_review identifies a file's health, the client could subscribe to that file resource. When the developer saves edits, the server sends a changed notification, the client re-calls code_health_review, and displays the updated score in real time — without the user having to re-invoke the tool. Limitation: resource subscriptions have low client support as of early 2026 (Claude Desktop does not support them; MCP Inspector does). The 2026 RC's ttlMs field provides an alternative: the server annotates results with a max cache TTL (e.g., 60 seconds), after which the client knows to refetch rather than use the cached score. This is a lower-friction alternative to subscriptions given current client gaps.
evidence: MCP spec: resources/subscribe + notifications/resources/updated protocol. Known limitation: 'very few clients actually support resource subscriptions since it's optional anyway — Claude Desktop does not support resource subscriptions, however, Inspector does.' 2026 RC alternative: ttlMs in response metadata.

title: Prompt caching now has two TTLs: 5-minute default and 1-hour option — with a critical 2026 isolation change
summary: Anthropic now offers two distinct prompt cache TTLs. The 5-minute TTL is the default (1.25x write, 0.1x read vs base input). The 1-hour TTL costs 2x base input for writes but still reads at 0.1x, making it worthwhile whenever a session generates >2 reads per hour. On February 5, 2026 Anthropic changed cache isolation from organization-level to workspace-level on the Claude API and AWS; Bedrock and Vertex AI still use org-level. A DEV.to analysis quantified that the switch to the shorter default TTL 'increased effective API costs by 30–60%' for production agentic workloads that had been relying on 60-minute hits. For the refactoring loop: a 10K-token system prompt (tool schemas + instructions) written once and read 20 times now costs $0.0435 vs $0.0975 under the old regime — a 55% reduction in caching benefit. The fix: explicitly set ttl=1h on the cache_control block for the system prompt and tool definitions. Important gotcha: the refactoring loop's followUpInstruction includes effort level hints that change per turn, which will bust the cache if placed before the breakpoint. Keep all mutable per-turn data after the last cache_control breakpoint. Also: up to 4 explicit cache breakpoints per request allow independent TTLs on different content segments.
evidence: Cache read price is 0.1x base input (90% off); 1h write is 2x base input; 5m write is 1.25x. Minimum cacheable prefix: 4096 tokens for Opus 4.x, 1024 tokens for Sonnet 4.6. Workspace isolation change on Feb 5, 2026 may cause unexpected cache misses in multi-workspace deployments.

title: Context Compaction API (compact-2026-01-12) achieves 87% active-context reduction for long refactoring loops
summary: The server-side compaction API, launched January 2026 and now supporting Opus 4.6/4.7/4.8 and Sonnet 4.6, automatically summarizes conversation history when input tokens exceed a configurable threshold (default 150K, minimum 50K). From the official documentation example: 180,000 input tokens compresses to ~23,000 (87% reduction). A custom summarization prompt (instructions field) can be provided — critically important for this project because the default behavior may cause the model to call tools during summarization instead of writing text. The recommended instructions explicitly prohibit tool calls during the summary step. Integration with prompt caching: add cache_control on compaction blocks and keep the system prompt's cache_control separate so it remains valid across compaction events. The remaining field in task_budget allows the budget countdown to carry forward across compaction cycles. Billing note: top-level usage.input_tokens excludes compaction iteration costs; must sum usage.iterations array for accurate billing.
evidence: Official docs example: 180K tokens → 23K tokens active context (87% reduction) with ~3,500 output tokens cost for the summarization step. Minimum trigger threshold 50K tokens. Beta header: compact-2026-01-12. Supports Opus 4.6+, Sonnet 4.6+.

title: Task Budgets beta (task-budgets-2026-03-13) gives Claude a self-regulating token countdown across the full agentic loop
summary: Task budgets on Opus 4.7 and 4.8 inject a server-side countdown marker that Claude uses to pace and finish gracefully. The budget spans thinking, tool calls, tool results, and output across all requests in the loop — not just a single turn. Minimum value is 20,000 tokens. The budget is advisory (soft cap), not enforced — max_tokens remains the hard per-request ceiling. Key interaction with the refactoring loop: the budget counts only what Claude sees this turn (new tool results + generated tokens), not resent prior history. This means prompt-cached turns cost almost nothing against the budget. The remaining field enables carry-forward across compaction. Critically, task_budget interacts with adaptive thinking: as budget depletes, Claude naturally reduces thinking token consumption. Do not decrement remaining client-side when resending full history — this double-counts and causes premature termination. Sizing guidance: measure p99 token spend per refactoring task without budget, then set budget at that level, using max_tokens as a hard backstop per request.
evidence: Official docs example: 3-turn agentic loop spent 19,000 budget tokens even though client sent ~20,820 cumulative input tokens. Budget minimum: 20,000 tokens. Works on Opus 4.7 and 4.8 only. Beta header: task-budgets-2026-03-13.

title: Tool Search Tool (advanced-tool-use-2025-11-20) reduces tool-definition overhead by 85% and improves accuracy
summary: With 27 tools already in the Healthy AI Code MCP server, tool definitions constitute a large fraction of every request's input tokens. The Tool Search Tool feature (beta header advanced-tool-use-2025-11-20) enables deferred loading: tools marked defer_loading: true are not transmitted in the initial request. Claude uses a tool_search_tool to discover and load tool schemas only when needed. Anthropic measured 58 tools consuming ~55K tokens before any work begins, reducible to ~8.7K tokens with Tool Search — an 85% reduction in tool-definition overhead. Accuracy improved: Claude Opus 4 went from 49% to 74%, Opus 4.5 from 79.5% to 88.1% on large tool catalog evaluations. This is particularly relevant for the Healthy AI Code MCP because a refactoring loop typically uses only 3-5 of the 27 tools per iteration. The tool_search_tool uses regex-based search (tool_search_tool_regex_20251119) to find relevant tools. Combine with tool use examples (input_examples array on tool definitions) which improved parameter accuracy from 72% to 90% in internal tests — zero token cost since examples replace ambiguous description prose.
evidence: Tool Search Tool: traditional 27+ tools ~55K tokens; with optimization ~8.7K tokens (85% reduction). Accuracy: Opus 4 49%→74%, Opus 4.5 79.5%→88.1%. Tool Use Examples (input_examples): 72%→90% parameter accuracy. Beta header: advanced-tool-use-2025-11-20.

title: Programmatic Tool Calling collapses N tool-call round-trips into ~2 inference passes, cutting costs up to 80%
summary: Programmatic Tool Calling allows Claude to write Python/JavaScript orchestration code that calls multiple tools sequentially or in parallel inside a code execution container. Intermediate results are processed within the container and only final outputs enter the model context. For a refactoring loop where each iteration involves code_health_review → analyze → code_health_auto_refactor → apply → re-review, this could collapse 5+ round-trips into 2. Anthropic measured: 43,588 tokens reduced to 27,297 tokens on complex multi-step tasks (37% savings), with 19+ inference passes eliminated for 20-tool workflows. Third-party implementation (cameronking4 on GitHub) reports 80% cost reduction in practice. Implementation requires adding the code_execution_20250825 tool type and marking eligible tools with allowed_callers: ['code_execution_20250825']. One caveat: this removes intermediate results from the model's context, which may reduce Claude's ability to self-correct mid-iteration for complex refactors — test empirically before enabling globally.
evidence: Official Anthropic measurement: 43,588→27,297 tokens on complex tasks (37% reduction). Third-party reports: up to 80% cost reduction (LLM roundtrips from N+1 to ~2 per subtask). 19+ inference passes eliminated for 20-tool orchestration. Requires code_execution_20250825 tool type.

title: Token-Efficient Tools beta reduces tool-response output tokens by an average 14%, up to 70% in best cases
summary: The token-efficient-tools-2025-02-19 beta header reduces the verbosity of tool-use response formatting, specifically shrinking the output token cost of tool_use and tool_result blocks. Anthropic reports: up to 70% reduction in output token consumption for tool-use responses in favorable cases, with an average of 14% across real workloads. This is already documented in the project's CLAUDE.md as a recommended tip. For a refactoring loop with many tool calls per iteration, 14% average output token savings is meaningful but not transformative. However, it requires zero code change beyond adding the header, making it strictly additive. Combined with structured outputs (which cache the tool schemas separately), the two betas stack.
evidence: Anthropic official: up to 70% output token reduction, average 14% in practice. Zero code change required. Available on Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI. Beta header: token-efficient-tools-2025-02-19.

title: Structured Outputs (now GA) provides constrained JSON decoding and 24-hour schema caching
summary: Structured outputs moved from beta (structured-outputs-2025-11-13) to GA via the output_config.format parameter. Constrained decoding compiles the JSON schema into a grammar and restricts token generation at inference time — the model cannot produce tokens that violate the schema. This has two benefits for the refactoring loop: (1) eliminates retry loops caused by malformed tool responses, saving wasted round-trips; (2) Anthropic caches compiled schemas for 24 hours, reducing per-call latency and schema-transmission overhead when the same tool (e.g., code_health_auto_refactor) is called dozens of times in a loop. The project already documents this feature, but the key new detail is that the schema compilation is cached server-side for 24 hours — relevant for long-running daily sessions where the same tool schema is used across hundreds of iterations.
evidence: Schema compilation cached 24 hours server-side. Constrained decoding: logit processor inserted between model output and sampling — schema violations are impossible. GA via output_config.format; beta path still works via structured-outputs-2025-11-13 header.

title: Fine-Grained Tool Streaming is now GA (no beta header needed) and reduces TTFT on large code-block tool inputs
summary: Fine-grained tool streaming (previously behind a beta header) is now generally available on Sonnet 4.6 and later, requiring no special header. It streams tool input parameters without server-side JSON buffering or validation, allowing the model to start reading large currentCode or focusLines parameters before the full JSON object is transmitted. The project CLAUDE.md already documents this for eager_input_streaming, noting 200–800ms TTFT reduction for large functions. The new detail: the feature is now GA, so no beta header is needed, removing one adoption barrier. For the refactoring loop, this primarily reduces wall-clock time rather than token count, but shorter latency improves the interactive feel when a human is watching the loop run.
evidence: Fine-grained tool streaming is now GA on Sonnet 4.6+ — no beta header required. Previously documented in project CLAUDE.md but required a beta header. 200–800ms TTFT reduction for large parameter blocks.

title: Adaptive Thinking effort parameter (low/medium/high/xhigh/max) cuts thinking token spend 40-60% without model switching
summary: Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7 replaced the legacy fixed-budget thinking API with an effort parameter. The model dynamically allocates thinking tokens based on perceived problem complexity. A task consuming 15,000 thinking tokens under a fixed 20K budget may use only 8,000 with adaptive thinking. Reported savings: 40-60% pipeline spend reduction. For the refactoring loop, the project CLAUDE.md already maps effort to nearTarget/successLikelihood, which is good practice. The new detail: effort=low (for simple classification/routing) is described as suitable for high-volume tasks like 'near target' refactors where the remaining smells are minor. The xhigh level is Opus 4.7-exclusive (falls back to high on 4.6). Adaptive thinking also naturally scales down as task_budget depletes — a synergistic interaction meaning the two features together reduce spending more than either alone.
evidence: Adaptive thinking vs fixed budget: 15K → 8K thinking tokens reported for same task (47% reduction). Pipeline spend reduction: 40-60% per AgentMarketCap analysis. Effort tiers: low/medium/high/xhigh/max. xhigh exclusive to Opus 4.7+. Interaction: adaptive thinking scales down as task_budget depletes.

title: Message Batches API offers 50% cost reduction with 24-hour turnaround — viable for offline health audits
summary: The Message Batches API processes up to 10,000 asynchronous requests with a 24-hour SLA at exactly 50% off standard input and output token prices. No quality difference vs real-time responses. For the Healthy AI Code MCP, this is not suitable for the interactive refactoring loop (which requires synchronous responses), but is directly applicable to: (1) the health-audit.mjs self-audit script that runs on all project files; (2) bulk onboarding analysis when a new codebase is first analyzed; (3) nightly scheduled audits via Claude Routines. Pricing: Opus 4.7 drops from $5/$25 to $2.50/$12.50 per MTok input/output; Sonnet 4.6 from $3/$15 to $1.50/$7.50. Supports up to 300K output tokens per request. Combining batch API with prompt caching is valid: cached prefixes still get the 0.1x read rate, stacking 50% batch discount with 90% cache read discount for frequently analyzed files.
evidence: 50% off all token prices. 24-hour SLA. Up to 10,000 requests per batch, up to 300K output tokens per request. Compatible with prompt caching (cache reads at 0.1x still apply within batch). Opus 4.7: $2.50/$12.50 per MTok batch pricing.

title: Context engineering pattern: strip completed-iteration tool results from the messages array to prevent context bloat
summary: Anthropic's 'Effective Context Engineering' post (2026) documents a specific pattern for agentic refactoring loops: after each loop iteration completes, remove the large tool_result blocks from earlier iterations from the messages array before the next API call. In a 6-iteration refactoring loop where each iteration carries 2K tokens of code_health_review output and 1K of auto_refactor output, not stripping means turn 6 carries ~18K tokens of accumulated tool results that are no longer needed for future decisions. The compaction API automates this but at the cost of a summarization step; manual selective stripping is cheaper and more precise. Specifically: keep the most recent code_health_review result and the last auto_refactor instruction, but drop all earlier tool results. This is complementary to, not a replacement for, compaction.
evidence: Anthropic engineering blog documents structured note-taking and selective tool-result removal as primary context management strategies for agentic loops. Compaction and memory tool handle automated variants. No quantified savings from this source, but mechanics are well-documented.

title: Structure-Aware Diff Format (FuncDiff/BlockDiff) cuts token cost 30%+ on long-code edits
summary: The paper 'To Diff or Not to Diff' (arXiv 2604.27296, April 2026) shows that conventional unified diffs with line numbers are unnatural for LLMs because 'fragmented hunks break syntactic integrity'. Block-level and function-level diff formats (BlockDiff, FuncDiff) that rewrite entire AST-coherent units match or exceed full-rewrite accuracy while reducing tokens and latency by 30%+ for code over 300 tokens. The adaptive AdaEdit selector (trained to pick the cheapest valid format per edit) achieves 90% format selection accuracy and 95% when allowing 20% token deviation. Applied to the Healthy AI Code MCP: the auto_refactor tool currently returns full code rewrites; switching to FuncDiff for functions >300 tokens would directly reduce loop token cost by ~30% on large files. This requires using AST-aware output rather than full-file replacement.
evidence: 30%+ reduction in both latency and cost for long-code editing tasks (code >300 tokens). AdaEdit achieves accuracy matching full-code generation on benchmarks; FuncDiff even exceeds full-code with capable models.

title: Pre-Act (plan-before-act) raises goal completion from 32% to 82% vs ReAct baseline
summary: Pre-Act (arXiv 2505.09970, May 2025) extends ReAct by generating a full n-step execution plan with per-step reasoning before taking any action. As each step executes, the plan is refined using accumulated context, enabling dynamic recovery when outcomes deviate. On the Almita dataset it improves action recall by 70% over ReAct and fine-tuned 70B achieves 82% goal completion vs 32% for GPT-4 with ReAct. Applied to this project: the refactoring loop should begin each session with an explicit multi-file plan (which smells to fix, in what order, predicted score delta per function) before issuing any code_health_auto_refactor calls. This front-loads reasoning, reduces mid-loop course corrections, and cuts wasted iterations. The 'followUpInstruction' in code_health_auto_refactor already encodes this partially; a dedicated plan step before the first tool call would complete the pattern.
evidence: 82% vs 32% goal completion (Almita dataset), 70% improvement in action recall. Fine-tuned 70B outperforms GPT-4 by 69.5% in action accuracy at turn level.

title: MANTRA RAG-injected refactoring: 82.8% compile+test success vs 8.7% raw-LLM baseline
summary: MANTRA (arXiv 2503.14340, March 2025) combines RAG over prior refactorings (BM25 + dense embeddings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion), 3 few-shot examples per call, caller/callee context injection, and a verbal RL self-repair loop (up to 20 repair attempts per function). Result: 82.8% success (compile + pass all tests) vs 8.7% for bare GPT calls. 50% improvement over IntelliJ's EM-Assist on Extract Method. The key novelty for this project: (1) storing past successful refactoring pairs as a retrieval corpus; (2) injecting 2-3 similar examples when generating the refactored code; (3) including direct callers and callees in the prompt, not just the target function. The project's code_health_auto_refactor instructions already send numbered steps; adding few-shot retrieval would push single-pass success rate substantially higher.
evidence: MANTRA: 582/703 (82.8%) successful refactorings vs 61/703 (8.7%) RawGPT; CodeBLEU 0.640 vs 0.517; human readability rating 4.15 vs 4.02 vs developer-written.

title: HAFixAgent: Git-blame history context improves multi-hunk fix rate by 190%+ on complex bugs
summary: HAFixAgent (arXiv 2511.01047, November 2025) injects three blame-derived heuristics into the repair loop context: fn_all (names of all functions co-changed), fn_pair (before/after snapshots of changed functions), fl_diff (complete git diffs). On BugsInPy Python bugs: +38.6% overall (377 vs 272 fixes), and for single-file multi-hunk bugs (SFMH): +190.7% (54 to 157 repairs). Robustness: when fault localization shifts by 5 lines, non-history agents collapse to 0% fix rate; history agents maintain 40-56%. Critically, history context does NOT increase step count or cost significantly. Applied to this project: the MethodTemporalCoupling smell already uses git history for detection. Extending git-blame context into the refactoring instructions (show the diff that introduced the smell, show co-changed functions) could dramatically improve fix quality on complex smells like BrainMethod and GodClass.
evidence: +190.7% fix rate on single-file multi-hunk bugs; +38.6% overall on Python bugs; robustness maintained at 40-56% under +5 line localization noise vs 0% without history.

title: CTRL critic model (RL-trained) enables 106% improvement in code generation via iterative critique-revision
summary: CTRL (arXiv 2502.03492, February 2025) trains a dedicated critic LLM via two-stage GRPO reinforcement learning to provide feedback that maximizes the probability of the generator model correcting code. The critic is decoupled from the generator (different model). Results: 106.1% relative improvement in Pass@1 on CodeContests via multi-turn critique-revision. The critic transfers: when integrated with GPT-4o as the generator, it improves Pass@1 by 23.5%. Applied to this project: the current loop uses the same model for both analysis and refactoring. Running a small, RL-trained critic model to evaluate the proposed refactoring against the identified smells before the apply step would identify likely failures before committing, potentially halving wasted iterations. This is architecturally feasible as a lightweight MCP tool called between auto_refactor instruction generation and code application.
evidence: 106.1% relative improvement in Pass@1 on CodeContests; +23.5% improvement when critic used with GPT-4o as generator; critic trained without human supervision.

title: Dual-LLM abstain+validate policy: up to 39pp higher signal quality, fewer wasted patches
summary: Abstain and Validate (arXiv 2510.03217, October 2025, accepted ICSE 2026) introduces two complementary filters: (1) bug abstention predicts whether the agentic system is likely to fix the issue at all; (2) patch validation rejects patches unlikely to be correct before presenting to a human reviewer. On 174 human-reported bugs: abstention alone +13pp precision, validation alone +15pp, combined +39pp. Applied to this project: the refactoring loop could use a lightweight plausibility check after code_health_auto_refactor returns instructions, scoring whether the proposed fix is likely to reduce the specific smell weights. Bugs/smells with low estimated fix probability could be skipped or routed to a different strategy, preventing wasted iterations on targets the model cannot fix mechanically.
evidence: Up to +39pp precision improvement on 174 bugs when abstention and validation policies combined; both policies individually add 13-15pp. ICSE 2026 accepted.

title: Meta-tools (AWO) reduce LLM inference calls 5.6-11.9% by bundling recurring tool sequences
summary: Agent Workflow Optimization (arXiv 2601.22037, January 2026) mines workflow execution traces to find high-frequency sequential tool call patterns and bundles them into single meta-tools that bypass intermediate LLM reasoning. Results: 5.6-11.9% fewer LLM calls, 4.2-15% cost reduction, 4.2pp task success improvement, 1.0-2.63 fewer trajectory steps. Applied to this project: the code_health_review -> code_health_auto_refactor sequence is extremely regular across iterations. Wrapping this pair (or the triple review-refactor-re-review) into a meta-tool that deterministically chains them would reduce per-iteration inference overhead. The project already documents programmatic tool calling for this purpose; AWO provides the theoretical grounding and methodology to discover which sub-sequences are worth bundling from actual loop traces.
evidence: 11.9% reduction in LLM calls, up to 15% cost reduction, 4.2pp task success improvement across two agentic benchmarks.

title: Probabilistic convergence theory: self-correction loops ceiling and convergence in 3-5 iterations
summary: Yang et al. EMNLP 2025 (arXiv 2508.16456) formalized self-correction as a Markov chain: accuracy after round t = Acc_t with ceiling Upp = CS / (1 - CL + CS) where CS = Critique Score (probability of fixing an error) and CL = Confidence Level (probability of not breaking a correct fix). Convergence rate alpha = CL - CS; smaller alpha = faster convergence. For current LLMs, convergence happens in 3-5 rounds. Applied to this project: this theory predicts that the current 2-6 iteration benchmark aligns with the theory's 3-5 round convergence. To push past the ceiling (score >9.5 reliably), you must improve CS (better structured instructions increase probability of fixing a given smell) rather than adding iterations. This validates the project's focus on instruction quality over iteration count.
evidence: Formal Markov chain model with convergence ceiling Upp = CS/(1-CL+CS); empirically confirmed 3-5 round convergence for current LLM families. Published EMNLP 2025.

title: RefAgent multi-agent architecture: 90% test pass rate, 52.5% smell reduction vs single-agent
summary: RefAgent (arXiv 2511.03153, November 2025) uses 4 specialized agents: Context-Aware Planner (identifies refactoring opportunities, generates structured plan), Developer (executes refactoring), Compiler/Tester (validates compilation and tests), and Reflector (self-reflective feedback when tests fail). Results vs single-agent: 90% median unit test pass rate (vs ~55% baseline), 52.5% code smell reduction, 8.6% improvement in quality attributes, 64.7% improvement in test pass rate over single-agent, 40.1% improvement in compilation success. The structured plan output specifically guides which functions to target and in what order. Applied to this project: the current loop is single-agent. Splitting into Planner (consumes health report, produces ordered smell-fix plan) + Executor (applies changes) + Verifier (re-runs code_health_review and checks score delta) would match RefAgent's architecture and likely improve one-pass success rates.
evidence: 90% median test pass rate; 52.5% code smell reduction; 64.7% improvement over single-agent test pass rate; 40.1% compilation success improvement.

title: SWE-Edit adaptive editor: 2.1% resolved rate gain + 17.9% cost reduction via format selection
summary: SWE-Edit (arXiv 2604.26102, April 2026) decomposes code editing into a Viewer subagent (extracts task-relevant code on demand) and an Editor subagent (executes modifications from high-level plans), trained with GRPO to adaptively choose between find-replace and whole-file rewrite. On SWE-Bench Verified: +2.1% resolved rate AND -17.9% inference cost simultaneously. The key insight is that optimal format varies by change size: small changes should use find-replace (minimal context), complex restructuring needs whole-file. Applied to this project: the code_health_auto_refactor tool currently returns a single format (numbered steps + skeleton). Adding a 'minimal edit' mode for simple smells (MagicNumber, early return) and a 'full function rewrite' mode only for complex smells (ComplexMethod, BrainMethod, GodClass) would reduce token overhead on simple fixes without sacrificing quality on hard ones.
evidence: +2.1% resolved rate, -17.9% inference cost on SWE-Bench Verified. Published April 2026.

title: Alves 2010 Benchmark-Based Threshold Derivation — The Canonical Method
summary: Alves et al. derive metric thresholds empirically from a large benchmark corpus rather than expert opinion, using four percentile bands: low (70th percentile), moderate (80th), high (90th), and very high (>90th). The method is driven by empirical distribution of code metric values, is robust to skew, and is repeatable and transparent. The 2024 Filo et al. replication on 3268 releases from 65 Java projects confirms these thresholds support fault prediction and bad-smell detection across 62 OO metrics. Critically, the Alves approach sets thresholds per metric independently — it does NOT address how to aggregate multiple metric signals into a single composite score (the step where Healthy AI Code's formula lives). The project's current Java-only calibration matches this lineage but does not yet use percentile-derived per-smell thresholds that trigger score penalties.
evidence: Filo et al. (2024) derived thresholds for 62 OO metrics using 5 threshold derivation methods on 65 Java projects, confirming predictive validity. Alves used 70th/80th/90th/>90th percentile bands.

title: SATT: Architecture-Specific Threshold Tailoring Invalidates Uniform Weights
summary: The SATT approach (IEEE 2016, still the state of the art as of 2025 literature) shows that applying uniform metric thresholds across all classes regardless of architectural role is invalid. A God Class threshold appropriate for a domain service is too strict for an orchestration facade, and too lenient for a value object. The same logic applies to the project's fixed weight table: a ComplexMethod weight of 1.5 is simultaneously too punitive for generated parser code and too lenient for a security-sensitive auth handler. Implementing role-aware weights — derived from which architectural layer a file belongs to — would make the 9.5 AI_READY threshold more meaningful. The project could infer role from directory/file naming conventions (e.g., 'controller', 'service', 'entity', 'util') without needing full architectural analysis.
evidence: SATT detects when an architectural role is considerably different from others in the system and provides a specific threshold for that role. Current tools do not take system architecture into account, assessing all classes similarly.

title: CodeScene Code Red Paper: r=−0.58 Validates 1-10 Score; Green Threshold Is 8.0, Not 9.0
summary: The CodeScene 'Code Red' empirical study (arXiv 2203.04374, 39 proprietary codebases, 30,737 files) is the closest published validation of a 1-10 code health scoring model to the Healthy AI Code project. Key calibration findings: (1) Pearson r = −0.58 between code health and issue resolution time — meaningful but not deterministic; (2) Alert (< 4.0) code has 15x more defects than Healthy; (3) The published Green/Healthy threshold in the Code Red paper is ≥ 8.0, not ≥ 9.0 or ≥ 9.5. Separately, the 2026 AI-readiness whitepaper (Borg et al.) raises the AI-safe refactoring zone to ≥ 9 citing lower LLM break rates. The project's AI_READY threshold of 9.5 is stricter than both published thresholds — this may be aspirational rather than empirically derived, and should be validated against actual defect and LLM break-rate data to avoid being either gameable or unreachable.
evidence: Code Red study: 30,737 files, 39 codebases. r=−0.58 correlation. Green threshold = 8.0, Alert = <4.0. 15x defect differential. AI paper raises threshold to 9 for AI refactoring safety.

title: Smell Co-occurrence Has Asymmetric Quality Impact: Cohesion/Size Affected, Coupling/Complexity Are Not
summary: A 2025 IET Software study (Imran et al., JavaScript web games) found that smell co-occurrence has a statistically significant impact on cohesion, size, and inheritance quality attributes, but no significant impact on coupling or complexity. This has a direct implication for scoring models: treating all smell interactions as independent and additive (which the project's current sum-of-penalties formula does) is defensible for coupling-related smells (FeatureEnvy, DataClumps) but under-weights co-occurring smells that share a cohesion or size dimension (GodClass + BrainMethod on the same file, for instance). A co-occurrence bonus penalty — incrementing the weight of a smell when another related smell is present on the same file — could better reflect the compounding quality impact without full multiplicative scoring.
evidence: Wilcoxon signed rank test showed p significant for cohesion, size, inheritance under co-occurrence; p not significant for coupling and complexity. Random forest classifier accuracy 99.1%.

title: Co-Change Graph Entropy: New Process Metric with Pearson r=0.54 and +10% AUROC When Combined
summary: A 2025 MSR/EASE paper introduces Co-Change Graph Entropy — a metric that models which files co-change together as a graph, then computes the entropy of that graph's community structure. On 8 Apache projects: standalone Pearson r = 0.54 with defect count; replacing change entropy with co-change entropy improved AUROC in 72.5% of cases; combining both improved AUROC in 82.5% of cases with statistically significant gains (Friedman + Nemenyi test). The project already tracks MethodTemporalCoupling using git co-change, but that is a per-method metric. File-level co-change graph entropy is complementary and captures structural co-change dispersion beyond what method coupling detects. This is a new biomarker candidate that could be added to the existing temporal analytics module.
evidence: 8 Apache projects, Pearson r up to 0.54, AUROC improvement 82.5% of 40 experimental settings when combined with change entropy. Statistical significance via Friedman + post-hoc Nemenyi.

title: Expected Calibration Error (ECE): JIT Defect Models Are 2–35% Miscalibrated — Same Risk Applies to Code Health Scores
summary: A 2025 MSR paper (arXiv 2504.12051) shows that all evaluated just-in-time defect prediction models are miscalibrated: ECE ranges 2–35%, with DeepJIT the worst offender and LApredict the least. Critically, post-calibration methods (e.g., Platt scaling) do not consistently fix this — only Platt scaling on DeepJIT and CodeBERT4JIT helps reliably. The implication for Healthy AI Code: the claim that a score of 9.5 is 'AI-ready' is a threshold assertion, not a calibrated probability. Without measuring ECE on the project's own scoring model, it is unknown whether a score of 9.3 is meaningfully different from 9.5 in practice. Adding a calibration measurement pipeline — comparing predicted score ranges against actual human-assessed quality or LLM refactoring outcomes — would ground the thresholds in evidence.
evidence: All JIT DP models miscalibrated. ECE 2–35%. Platt scaling helps some models. Miscalibration risk is structural in any ML-based or rule-weighted scoring system claiming threshold-based guarantees.

title: Smell-Specific High-Correlation Features for Detection: LOC+WMC for GodClass, MAXNESTING+LOC for LongMethod
summary: A 2025 arXiv study (2510.05835) using Pearson correlation-based feature selection on 74 systems found that the most predictive features per smell type are: GodClass — LOC_type and WMC_type; DataClass — LCOM5 and NOPK; FeatureEnvy — FDP_method and ATFD_method; LongMethod — MAXNESTING_method and LOC_method; LongParameterList — NOP_method and LOC_method; SwitchStatements — LOC_method and MAXNESTING_method. Feature selection used a relative threshold: only features with correlation above dataset average were retained. This confirms that MAXNESTING is a top-2 predictor for both LongMethod and SwitchStatements — validating that the project's DeepNesting weight (1.2) is placed correctly. However, LCOM5 as a top predictor for DataClass is a metric the project does not currently expose as a smell.
evidence: 6 smells detected from 74-system Fontana dataset. Relative correlation threshold. Gradient Boosting: 99% accuracy on GodClass/LongMethod, 94% on LongParameterList. LCOM5 top feature for DataClass.

title: Goodhart's Law / Gameable Metrics: The √count Damper Mitigates But Doesn't Solve the Problem
summary: The project's √count damper in the scoring formula (score = 10 − Σ(weight × √count)) reduces marginal penalty for additional instances of a smell, which is a partial Goodhart-mitigation: a refactorer who splits one GodClass into two medium-sized classes avoids the full penalty. However, the formula is still gameable in a different direction: splitting one ComplexMethod (weight 1.5, count 1 → penalty 1.5) into three slightly-below-threshold methods (count 3, penalty 1.5×√3=2.6) actually makes the score worse. More critically, extracting dead helper methods to push a class below a LOC threshold but keep behavior in private methods is not detectable with current biomarkers. The mitigation: adding a 'test coverage proxy' smell (undocumented public methods, no test file co-located) and an 'extraction residue' smell (single-use private methods below threshold) would make the 9.5 target harder to game through superficial splits.
evidence: Goodhart's Law well-documented in software metric literature. √count formula is a standard sub-linear damper from econometrics. Gaming via method splitting is a known anti-pattern in automated refactoring evaluations.

title: LLM Code Smell Detection: High Precision But Low Recall (GPT-4.0: P=0.79, R=0.41) — Hybrid Approach Needed
summary: A 2025 EASE benchmark (arXiv 2504.16027) compared GPT-4.0 against DeepSeek-V3 for code smell detection across Java, Python, JS, C++. GPT-4.0 achieved precision 0.79 / recall 0.41 / F1 0.54; DeepSeek-V3 was much worse (F1 0.35). Both models had near-zero F1 for FeatureEnvy and ChangePreventers. GPT-4.0 was near-perfect for LargeClass (0.95/0.95) and MessageChains (1.00 F1). Implication for Healthy AI Code: using an LLM to verify or supplement the rule-based smell detection (especially for nuanced smells like FeatureEnvy where the current tree-sitter approach also struggles) could increase recall, but LLMs alone are not reliable enough to replace deterministic detection. A hybrid where the MCP returns the rule-based score and the LLM verifies edge cases is the right architecture.
evidence: GPT-4.0: P=0.79, R=0.41, F1=0.54. FeatureEnvy: F1=0.00 for both LLMs. LargeClass: 0.95/0.95. DeepSeek-V3: P=0.42, R=0.31, F1=0.35. Cost ~$0.04 per 114-line file for GPT-4.0.

title: Smell Impact Hierarchy from 2025 Large-Scale Empirical Study: High vs Low Impact Smells
summary: The 2025 Rahman et al. SPE study (13 smells, 35 open-source systems, 25 quality metrics) established that not all smells have equal impact. High-impact smells: LongMethod, AntiSingleton, ComplexClass, LargeClass, LongParameterList. Moderate: RefusedParentBequest, SpaghettiCode, Blob. Low impact: remaining smells. The project's current weight table partially reflects this (ComplexMethod 1.5, GodClass 1.5) but the 'LowMaintainability' smell weight is not explicitly listed in CLAUDE.md. Critically, AntiSingleton (high impact) is not a current biomarker — it refers to classes with multiple instances maintained through static state, creating hidden coupling. This could be added to TypeScript/JS analysis via detection of static mutable class fields with no factory pattern.
evidence: 35 open-source systems, 13 smells, 25 quality metrics. Long Method, Anti Singleton, Complex Class, Large Class confirmed high impact. Not all smells have equal impact — justifies non-uniform weighting.

title: SQALE Normalization as Alternative Scoring Paradigm: Time-Based Remediation Cost
summary: The SQALE method normalizes code quality as remediation cost in developer-hours divided by development cost (Technical Debt Ratio). SonarQube grades: A ≤ 5% TDR, E > 50% TDR. This is a fundamentally different paradigm from the project's 1–10 score: SQALE is continuous, time-based, and explainable in business terms ('2 hours of debt'). The project could expose a parallel SQALE-like metric: estimated minutes-to-fix per smell instance (e.g., ComplexMethod: 30 min, GodClass: 120 min) as a supplemental output from code_health_review. This would not replace the 1–10 score (which is better for loop convergence) but would make the score more auditable — a score of 8.5 would be accompanied by '~45 min of debt remaining' — helping users calibrate whether the 9.5 target is worth pursuing on a given file.
evidence: SQALE TDR = (Remediation Effort / Development Effort) × 100. SonarQube: A ≤ 5%, E > 50%. Remediation functions must be calibrated per organization. Parallel metric doesn't change loop behavior.

title: Five LLM Integration Code Smells (SpecDetect4AI / SATD paper, 2512.18020)
summary: A rigorously validated catalog of five code smells specific to code that *calls* LLM APIs — not just AI-generated code, but any codebase that integrates LLM inference. Smells: (1) Unbounded Max Metrics (UMM) — missing max_output_tokens, timeout, or max_retries on API calls; 38% of 200 open-source systems; 86.4% detection precision. (2) No Model Version Pinning (NMVP) — using moving aliases like 'gpt-4o' instead of dated versions; 36% of systems; 95.7% precision. (3) No System Message (NSM) — chat-based calls without a system role; 34.5% of systems; 85.7% precision. (4) No Structured Output (NSO) — API calls without a response_format schema; 40.5% of systems; 80% precision. (5) Temperature Not Explicitly Set (TNES) — omitting temperature on completion calls; 36.5% of systems; 82.6% precision.
