Detection tool SpecDetect4AI uses a Lark-based DSL that compiles into AST-traversal matchers with 52 reusable semantic predicates. Overall: 60.5% of 200 systems have at least one smell; 86.06% average precision across all five. These are structurally detectable via regex/AST on Python/TypeScript/JavaScript without runtime execution.
evidence: 60.5% of 200 open-source LLM systems carry at least one smell; validated on 826 systems in the broader SpecDetect4AI study; 86.06% avg detection precision. These five smells are completely absent from the project's current 28-biomarker catalog.

title: 22 ML-Pipeline AI-Specific Code Smells (SpecDetect4AI full catalog, 2509.20491)
summary: The broader SpecDetect4AI paper catalogs 22 smells across ML pipeline stages (Data Cleaning, Model Training, Model Evaluation, Feature Engineering). Top by volume: Randomness Uncontrolled / R2 (32,472 instances, 37.4% of all hits) — no seed set for numpy/torch/random before training; Data Leakage / R11 (19%, train/val split after transformation that sees test data); Deterministic Algorithm Not Used / R6 (12%). Other high-value smells: Gradients Not Cleared (R9), Memory Not Freed (R10), Hyperparameter Not Explicitly Set (R5), Threshold-Dependent Validation (R19), NaN Equivalence Comparison Misused (R18). Tool detected 86,910 instances across 25,311 files with 88.66% precision and 88.89% recall. DSL rule syntax is published. The smells target Python (PyTorch, TensorFlow, pandas) primarily — relevant for the project's Python Tier A support. A subset (R2, R5, R6, R10, R18, R19) are detectable without framework-specific introspection, using pure AST pattern matching.
evidence: 86,910 instances detected across 826 real open-source AI systems. Precision 88.66%, recall 88.89%. Published DSL rules and replication package. None of these 22 smells overlap with the project's current biomarker set.

title: KCH Hallucination Detection via AST + Library Introspection (arXiv 2601.19106)
summary: A deterministic post-processing framework detects Knowledge Conflicting Hallucinations (KCHs) — subtle semantic errors like non-existent API parameters that evade linters. Three categories: (1) Missing Imports (bare function calls without module prefix); (2) Mis-typed API Calls (misspellings like pd.read_exel); (3) Contextual Mismatches (semantically invalid calls like pd.read_excel('file.csv')). Detection: parse code to AST, extract import alias mappings, build a dynamic Knowledge Base via library introspection (enumerate public callables at import time), cross-reference call sites. Results on 200 Python snippets: 100% precision (0 false positives), 87.6% recall (F1=0.934). Auto-correction rate: 77% — highest on missing imports (97.9%), lowest on contextual mismatches (0%). Parallel static analysis study (arXiv 2604.07755) shows Pyright detects 14–85% of library hallucinations across GPT-4/GPT-3.5/CodeLlama datasets. Actionable: a new 'HallucinatedApiCall' biomarker could flag calls to non-existent methods on imported modules using a cached introspection KB — implementable in Python Tier A via tree-sitter + runtime introspection fallback.
evidence: 100% precision, 87.6% recall on 200 Python LLM-generated code samples. Complementary study shows static tools detect 14–85% of library hallucinations. 'Slopsquatting' supply chain attack vector validates urgency: ~5.2% of commercial LLM-generated package references are hallucinated, 21.7% for open-source models.

title: Package Hallucination as a Quantifiable Biomarker (arXiv 2501.19012 + Rescana report)
summary: LLMs hallucinate package references at measurable rates: 5.2% of packages in commercial model (GPT-4) output do not exist in PyPI/npm; 21.7% for open-source models (CodeLlama, DeepSeek, WizardCoder). Study generated 2.23M code samples, found 200K+ unique hallucinated names. 38% of hallucinated names are inspired by real packages, 13% are typos, 51% are fully fabricated. The slopsquatting attack: threat actors register these names with malicious code. Detection approach: after code analysis, cross-check every import/require statement against a cached registry snapshot (PyPI Simple API, npm registry search). This is a lightweight O(n) check on import nodes from the tree-sitter AST — no runtime needed. Could be implemented as a new 'HallucinatedPackageImport' biomarker with weight >= 1.5 given the supply chain security implication. The check is trivially extensible to Cargo.toml (Rust), go.mod (Go), Gemfile (Ruby), pyproject.toml.
evidence: 2.23M code samples analyzed; 5.2% hallucination rate for GPT-4, 21.7% for open-source LLMs. 200K+ unique hallucinated package names identified. Real supply chain attacks ('slopsquatting') documented in 2025.

title: GenAI-Induced SATD (GIST) — New Comment Pattern Biomarker (arXiv 2601.07786)
summary: Empirical study of 6,540 AI-referencing code comments from GitHub (Nov 2022–Jul 2025) identified 81 GIST instances where developers admit debt induced by AI tools. Two defining characteristics: (1) Knowledge Deficit — developer integrates AI code without understanding it, deferring validation; (2) Lack of Trust — uncertainty shifts verification responsibility to others. Debt distribution: Design Debt 40.7%, Requirement Debt 21%, Test Debt 21%, Defect Debt 13.6%, Documentation Debt 3.7%. AI is 'Source' of debt in 27.2% of cases (direct errors/redundant logic). Detection method: two-filter approach — first match AI tool name keywords (ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Claude, LLM + generated/suggested/written by/from/with/using), then match SATD markers (TODO, FIXME, HACK, XXX). The 1.47% intersection rate means most AI-referencing comments are benign — low false-positive concern. Actionable: extend existing SATD detection with a 'GiST' pattern that flags TODO/FIXME comments containing AI tool references, weighted separately from generic SATD. Cohen's kappa 0.896 between annotators validates taxonomy reliability.
evidence: 6,540 real GitHub comments analyzed; 81 confirmed GIST instances; Cohen's kappa 0.896 inter-annotator agreement. Project already has SATD detection but lacks the AI-attribution sub-classification.

title: Cognitive Debt and Intent Debt — New Debt Conceptual Layer (arXiv 2603.22106 + Addy Osmani / ThoughtWorks)
summary: Margaret Storey (2026) introduces 'Triple Debt' framing: traditional Technical Debt + Cognitive Debt (growing gap between codebase and team's mental model when AI generates code faster than humans can absorb) + Intent Debt (missing rationale behind AI-generated changes — the AI never went through the reasoning process, so the understanding lives nowhere). Thoughtworks Technology Radar (2025) lists 'Codebase Cognitive Debt' as a technique to watch. Addy Osmani's widely-cited article (2025) quantifies the problem: AI generates an order of magnitude more code per day than a human, compressing the time available to form understanding. Proxy detectors for cognitive/intent debt: (1) high comment-to-code ratio that is pure 'what' not 'why' (no rationale in comments); (2) functions with zero docstring or doc-comment near a SATD marker; (3) large functions with no inline comments (long method + zero explanatory comments = likely unreviewed AI dump); (4) churn rate spike after AI-attributed commits. While not all detectable by static analysis, proxies (1)–(3) are. This provides justification for a new 'MissingRationale' biomarker distinct from existing KnowledgeLoss.
evidence: Published arXiv March 2026 by Margaret Storey. Thoughtworks Radar endorsement. Addy Osmani article widely cited in industry (Medium + personal blog). The project's existing KnowledgeLoss biomarker is git-history-based (bus factor); this is a static-analysis-detectable proxy distinct from it.

title: LLM-Generated Code Has 63% More Implementation Smells Than Human Code (arXiv 2510.03029)
summary: Quantified the smell gap across 4 mainstream LLMs vs. human reference solutions. Findings: Codex worst (+84.97% more violations), ChatGPT +65.05%, Gemini Pro +62.07%, Falcon +42.28% (average +63.34%). Implementation smells (naming inconsistency, excessive complexity, magic numbers, dead code) are 73.35% higher on average; design smells (abstraction, encapsulation, modularization) are 21.42% higher. Scenario analysis: LLM code degrades most on encapsulation tasks (+138.5%), array manipulation (+101.9%), and OOP (+101.9%). Key finding: functional correctness does not predict code quality — a test suite pass does not mean health score pass. Detection tools used: PMD, Checkstyle, DesigniteJava. This validates the project's core premise (score != correctness) and suggests that the 63% average violation premium is a reproducible benchmark against which the project's scoring accuracy could be calibrated. Also: the Reasoning-Complexity Paradox from arXiv 2605.02741 — more capable models produce MORE bloated code (Long Method, God Class, high RFC) — means the project's ComplexMethod and GodClass biomarkers are the most impactful for AI-generated code specifically.
evidence: Quantitative comparisons across 4 LLMs vs. professional baselines. Correlation coefficient >0.93 between task complexity and smell prevalence. Project's existing biomarkers (ComplexMethod, GodClass) are validated as the highest-signal detectors for AI code.

title: Modular Mirage and PAU — Two Novel Architecture-Level AI Smells (arXiv 2605.02741)
summary: Agent-driven development introduces two smells not in traditional catalogs: (1) Modular Mirage — files are separated (superficial modularity) but lack semantic cohesion; manifests as Scattered Functionality (SF) and Unstable Dependencies (UD) that co-occur statistically; TLoC-to-architectural-smell correlation rho=0.94, p<0.001 makes total project LoC a near-perfect predictor of architectural decay in AI-generated repos. (2) Potential Improper API Usage (PAU) — agents rewrite external interaction logic inline rather than encapsulating reusable helpers, mirroring copy-paste coding; consistently high across all complexity stages. Third notable pattern: God Class Syndrome in AI code manifests as 'manager' classes with Too Many Branches (TMB) and High Response for a Class (RFC). Detection tool: PyExamine for Python. The TLoC/architectural-smell law is actionable: for project repos with large AI-generated files, a 'LargeFile + high coupling' compound biomarker could be introduced. PAU is partially detectable as duplicated import-and-usage blocks across files (a new variant of the existing duplicate code detection).
evidence: 20 AI-generated repos across 5 scenarios; TLoC–smell correlation rho=0.94 (p<0.001). PAU prevalence consistent across all complexity stages. Prompt specificity had no statistical impact on smell count (p>0.8), confirming smell accumulation is structural not prompt-driven.

title: LLM SATD in Projects Built With LLMs — Three Unique Debt Types (arXiv 2601.06266)
summary: First empirical SATD study comparing 477 repos: LLM-software, ML-software, and traditional software. LLM repos stay debt-free 2.4x longer (median 492 days vs. 204 days for ML repos) but then accumulate rapidly — the 'cliff' pattern. Three debt types unique to LLM projects: (1) Model-Stack Workaround Debt — hacks accommodating framework-specific bugs (LangChain API changes, prompt template breaks); (2) Model Dependency Debt — tight coupling to specific model providers/versions creating migration risk; (3) Performance Optimization Debt — deferred token/cost optimization, often left as TODO comments. PromptDebt study (arXiv 2509.20497) adds: Prompt Debt (6.61% of LLM SATD), LLM-Hyperparameter Debt (4.51%), LLM-Framework Debt (4.31%), Cost Debt (2.1%). Detection: SATDDetector ML classifier + LLM-keyword augmentation achieves 92.5% accuracy on validation set. Actionable: 'ModelDependencyDebt' biomarker detectable via hardcoded model name strings (e.g., 'gpt-4', 'claude-3', 'llama-3') in non-config source files — related to NMVP smell above but broader.
evidence: 477 repos analyzed; LLM repos show 2.4x longer debt-free period followed by cliff-pattern accumulation. SATDDetector achieves 92.5% classification accuracy. PromptDebt study uses Cohen's kappa 0.74 for taxonomy validation.

title: SonarQube AI Code Assurance — Competitor Benchmarks and Quality Gate Thresholds
summary: SonarSource reports 42% of committed code is now AI-generated or AI-assisted (2025). Their 'Sonar way for AI Code' quality gate uses: 80% new code coverage, 3% max duplicated lines (vs. project's score-based approach), cognitive complexity threshold 15 (reducible to 8 for 'hardened' profiles). SonarQube now integrates MCP protocol for Claude Code / Cursor — scanning against project rules before human review. Key competitive insight: SonarQube's AI-specific additions focus on (a) lowered complexity thresholds, (b) stricter deduplication, (c) security rule activation for AI-common patterns (injection, hardcoded creds, weak crypto). The project already covers most of these via existing biomarkers. The key gap: SonarQube does NOT detect the five LLM-integration smells (UMM, NMVP, NSM, NSO, TNES) — an opportunity to differentiate. SonarQube also does not detect package hallucinations (KCH) or GIST patterns.
evidence: SonarSource internal data: 42% of committed code is AI-assisted (2025). Quality gate thresholds documented. MCP integration confirmed. SonarQube does not catalog LLM-integration smells or KCH — confirmed gap vs. project roadmap.

title: LLM-Hybrid Secret Detection: Regex + Fine-tuned LLM Classification Pipeline
summary: The current project already detects HardcodedCredential and HardcodedApiKey via regex/heuristics. A 2025 arXiv study (arxiv.org/abs/2504.18784) demonstrates that augmenting regex with a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.1 8B or Mistral-7B classifier achieves F1=0.9852 (binary) and 0.9820 accuracy (multiclass) across 8 secret categories — private keys, API keys/secrets, auth tokens, database URLs, passwords, usernames. The pipeline: 761 predefined regex patterns extract candidates, each with 200-char context window, fed to the LLM. A separate study (arXiv 2510.18601, SecretLoc) found 4,828 secrets missed by all regex/entropy tools in 42.5% of 5,000 Google Play apps, including 10+ previously undetected types (OpenAI API keys, GitHub tokens, JWT tokens, RSA private keys). The key gap in the project: contextual LLM re-classification step after regex extraction. This would catch generic high-entropy strings that are not real secrets (false positives) and real secrets with non-standard patterns (false negatives). Open-source models (LLaMA-3.1 8B) are viable locally, preserving MCP's air-gap posture.
evidence: Fine-tuned LLaMA-3.1 8B: F1=0.9852, precision=0.9861, recall=0.9853. Mistral-7B multiclass: 0.9820 accuracy. Database/Server URL category: F1=1.0000. SecretLoc found 4,828 secrets missed by all prior tools in a corpus of 5,000 apps.

title: AI-Generated Code ('Vibe Coding') Specific Biomarkers: New CWE Cluster
summary: CSA research (2025-2026) quantifies that AI-assisted commits expose secrets at 2.13x the rate of human commits (3.2% vs 1.5%), and 65% of 1,400 production vibe-coded apps had security issues. Veracode's study of 100+ LLMs found 45% of tasks introduce vulnerabilities. Three CWEs are statistically overrepresented in AI-generated code vs human-authored code: CWE-639 (Insecure Direct Object Reference, 1.91x more likely), CWE-257 (Improper Password Handling/Storage, 1.88x more likely), and CWE-502 (Insecure Deserialization, 1.82x more likely). Additionally, 100% of 15 tested vibe-coded apps failed CSRF and security-headers checks. A new attack class called 'slopsquatting' — AI hallucinating package names that attackers register as malicious packages — represents a novel static-analysis biomarker: detect import/require statements referencing packages not in major registries (npm, PyPI, Maven). A second new class: hidden Unicode characters in .cursor/rules or copilot settings files that backdoor code generation (CVE-2025-53773, the 'Rules File Backdoor'). The project should add: InsecureDirectObjectReference, InsecureDeserializationRisk, CsrfMissingProtection, MissingSecurityHeaders, and SlopsquattingPackageReference biomarkers.
evidence: AI code has 2.74x more security issues per PR, 3.2% vs 1.5% secret leak rate, 65% of 1,400 production apps had security issues. CVEs attributed to AI code: 6 in Jan 2026, 35 in Mar 2026. CWE-639 at 1.91x, CWE-257 at 1.88x, CWE-502 at 1.82x prevalence vs human code.

title: OWASP Top 10 2025 Gap: Software Supply Chain Failures (A03) and Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (A10)
summary: OWASP Top 10:2025 (released Nov 2025, finalized Jan 2026, covering 175K+ CVEs across 248 CWEs) introduces two new categories absent from the project's current biomarker set. A03: Software Supply Chain Failures replaces 'Vulnerable and Outdated Components' and now covers compromised dependencies, malicious packages, tampered builds, insecure update mechanisms. A10: Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions captures verbose error messages leaking sensitive data (stack traces, file paths, internal hostnames), inadequate exception handling leading to inconsistent state, and systems that fail open rather than closed. The project already flags some security patterns but has no biomarker for: (1) bare except/catch-all handlers that swallow exceptions silently (MissingErrorHandling), (2) exception handlers that log or print sensitive context (SensitiveDataInException), or (3) dependency manifest analysis for suspicious packages. Additionally, SSRF was consolidated into Broken Access Control — the project's existing XssRisk and SqlInjectionRisk biomarkers don't cover SSRF (server-side HTTP requests constructed from user input). SsrfRisk is a concrete gap. Semgrep mapped all 4,000+ rules to the new OWASP 2025 taxonomy.
evidence: OWASP Top 10:2025 analyzed 175,000+ CVEs with 248 CWEs. A03 is entirely new. A10 is entirely new. SSRF moved into A01 Broken Access Control. Three categories renamed. Security Misconfiguration rose from #5 to #2, affecting 3% of tested applications.

title: VIVID: Vulnerability Data Flow Graph Prioritization for SAST Findings
summary: The VIVID paper (arXiv 2505.16205) addresses a critical problem for the project's scoring model: not all detected smells are equally harmful, but the current formula treats smell count uniformly within each type. VIVID graphs application vulnerability data flows (VDFs) as directed graphs, then applies graph-theory metrics to prioritize which files need remediation most urgently. Key metrics: out-degree and betweenness centrality identify files where sanitization is likely missing (taint sources and sanitizer locations); out-eigenvector centrality and PageRank identify sink files where vulnerabilities land. This maps cleanly onto the project's refactoring loop: instead of treating all SecurityRisk smells equally, a VDF-aware smell type could distinguish between 'taint source' (where unsanitized input enters) and 'taint sink' (where it's consumed in a dangerous call). In the context of the scoring formula score = 10 - Σ(weight × √count), a taint-source smell could have weight 1.0 while a confirmed taint-path smell (source-to-sink confirmed) could be weight 1.5-2.0. This would produce more actionable fix prioritization and reduce the loop iterations needed to clear security debt by focusing effort on dataflow-confirmed vulnerabilities first.
evidence: VIVID evaluated 9 graph theory metrics on deliberately insecure applications. Out-degree, betweenness centrality, in-eigenvector centrality, and cross-clique connectivity best identify refactoring candidates. Out-eigenvector centrality and PageRank identify vulnerability sinks.

title: Cryptographic Misuse Detection: CryptoAPI-Bench Class of Biomarkers
summary: The project has no dedicated cryptographic misuse biomarker beyond HardcodedApiKey/HardcodedCredential. Well-studied SAST targets in this domain include: weak cipher algorithm (MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4, 3DES used for security — CWE-327), hardcoded IV/nonce in symmetric encryption (CWE-329), predictable random number generation for security context (Math.random() in JS, random.random() in Python for tokens/keys — CWE-338), insufficient key length (RSA < 2048, AES < 128 bits — CWE-326), and missing TLS validation (accepting all certs, empty trust managers — CWE-295). A 2024 arXiv study (arXiv 2409.06561) benchmarked ChatGPT vs. CryptoGuard on Java crypto misuse: ChatGPT achieved 94.6% average F-measure after prompt engineering, outperforming CryptoGuard on predictable key detection (92.43% vs 76.92%). The project already uses tree-sitter AST for Tier A languages (TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, Go, Ruby, Rust, PHP, Kotlin, Scala) — these all have well-defined patterns for crypto API calls that can be detected at AST level: crypto module imports, specific cipher names, key sizes. This is a high-impact, tractable addition given existing AST infrastructure.
evidence: ChatGPT F-measure 94.6% on Java crypto misuse after prompt engineering vs CryptoGuard 76.92% on predictable keys. CWE-327 (broken crypto algorithms), CWE-338 (inadequate randomness) are well-established SAST targets. SpotBugs+FindSecBugs, CogniCrypt, CryptoGuard all implement these checks.

title: Supply Chain Attack Biomarkers: Malicious Package Patterns and SBOM-Adjacent Detection
summary: OWASP A03:2025 (Supply Chain Failures) represents the project's most significant coverage gap for the 2025-2026 threat landscape. The March 2026 Axios npm attack (maintainer account hijack), September 2025 GhostAction attack (570+ repositories, 3,300+ secrets), and the self-replicating Shai-Hulud npm worm demonstrate that supply chain compromise is now #3 on OWASP. For a code-health MCP, three static detection strategies are tractable: (1) Package manifest scanning — parse package.json/requirements.txt/Cargo.toml/go.mod and flag packages with recent ownership changes, no homepage, single-commit history, or that match known malicious pattern lists (Datadog's GuardDog tool uses this heuristic). (2) Import analysis — detect imports of packages that reference both network I/O and file system access in the same module without clear justification (indicators of exfiltration logic). (3) Typosquat/slopsquat detection — compare imported package names against Levenshtein distance of top-N registry packages; flag names within edit distance 2 of popular packages. These are Tier B/C analysis techniques (regex/structural) applicable to 40+ of the project's supported languages via their package manifest formats. Supply chain attack surface increased 3x YoY as of 2025.
evidence: 97% of AI projects contain vulnerable dependencies. Supply chain attacks up 3x YoY. March 2026 Axios npm hijack: RAT deployed on npm install. September 2025 GhostAction: 570+ repos, 3,300+ secrets stolen. 20% of AI-generated code references non-existent packages (slopsquatting vector).

title: Path Traversal (CWE-22) AST-Level Detection Gap
summary: A May 2025 arXiv study (arXiv 2505.20186) scanned GitHub for a specific CWE-22 path traversal pattern and found 1,756 vulnerable open-source projects, demonstrating both prevalence and tractability of static detection. The project currently lacks a PathTraversalRisk biomarker. Path traversal via AST: detect cases where user-controlled input (function parameters, request object fields) flows into file path construction (os.path.join, fs.readFile, open(), File(), path.resolve()) without sanitization (basename, realpath, normalize with root validation). This is fully tractable with tree-sitter AST for Tier A languages. Key patterns per language: Python: os.path.join with request.args/form, open(user_input); JS/TS: fs.readFile/createReadStream with req.params/query; Java: new File(userInput); Go: os.Open with r.URL.Query(); PHP: file_get_contents with $_GET/$_POST. At tree-sitter level this requires identifying function call nodes where an argument traces back to a parameter/request field — a simplified single-function taint trace (no inter-procedural analysis required for common cases). The Sonar taint analysis engine already does this for CWE-22.
evidence: 1,756 vulnerable open-source projects found with automated CWE-22 path traversal scanning across GitHub. Pattern is detectable with static regex/AST analysis. Sonar taint engine covers this. Semgrep has rules for this pattern across all major languages.

title: Insecure Deserialization (CWE-502) Detection for Tier A Languages
summary: Insecure deserialization appears in OWASP Top 10:2025 (within Injection, A05) and is 1.82x more prevalent in AI-generated code vs human code. The project lacks a dedicated InsecureDeserializationRisk biomarker. Detection at AST level is well-specified: Python: pickle.load/loads, yaml.load (without Loader=yaml.SafeLoader), marshal.load, shelve with untrusted input; JS/TS: eval(JSON.parse()), node-serialize, serialize-javascript, vm.runInNewContext with user data; Java: ObjectInputStream.readObject() on untrusted streams, XStream without security configuration, Jackson with default typing enabled; PHP: unserialize() with user-controlled input; Ruby: Marshal.load, YAML.load (not YAML.safe_load); Go: encoding/gob.Decode with untrusted data. All of these are function-call patterns detectable at tree-sitter AST level without inter-procedural taint analysis — match the function name at call sites. Weight suggestion: 1.2-1.5 (equivalent to DeepNesting/BrainMethod), since it's a confirmed dangerous API pattern but not always exploitable without context. The Sonar taint engine documentation confirms this is a standard taint sink category.
evidence: CWE-502 is 1.82x more prevalent in AI-generated code vs human code (CSA 2025). Java: ObjectInputStream.readObject() is the canonical pattern. Python: pickle.load is well-documented. All patterns are simple call-site matches in AST — no inter-procedural analysis needed for initial detection.

title: Reachability Analysis for Security Smell Weight Calibration (Reducing False Positives)
summary: The current project scores all detected instances of a smell type equally via the √count formula. For security smells specifically, this causes noise: a SqlInjectionRisk detected in a unit test harness with mock data has the same weight impact as one in a production request handler. The 2025-2026 SAST market has converged on reachability analysis as the key false-positive reducer — Endor Labs, Konvu, and Mend SAST all report 90-95% noise reduction when reachability is applied. For the project's MCP context, a tractable version of reachability: (1) detect if the flagged function/method is only called from test files (path contains /test/, /spec/, /mock/, /__tests__/) and halve the smell weight, (2) detect if the flagged code is inside a conditional block that can only execute with a debug/dev environment flag (NODE_ENV check, DEBUG constant), (3) detect if a dangerous sink (eval, unserialize, etc.) receives only string literals rather than variable inputs. These heuristics are implementable at tree-sitter AST level without full inter-procedural dataflow. Even a basic test-context filter would substantially improve score accuracy for production files vs test files.
evidence: Reachability analysis reduces SAST noise by 90-95% according to Endor Labs and Konvu 2026 comparisons. Mend SAST exploitability engine goes beyond reachability with AI-based prioritization. Industry consensus: false positives are the #1 adoption blocker for SAST in 2025.

title: OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 Biomarkers: Prompt Injection Patterns in Application Code
summary: The OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 is now a distinct compliance target for applications that integrate LLMs. The project has no biomarkers for LLM-specific code risks. Statically detectable patterns include: LLM01 (Prompt Injection) — user input concatenated directly into prompt strings without sanitization (f-string/template-literal prompt construction with request parameters); LLM06 (Excessive Agency) — LLM tool calls given filesystem, shell, or database permissions without confirmation gates (detecting tool definitions with broad permissions in code); LLM07 (System Prompt Leakage) — system prompt returned in API response or logged; LLM05 (Improper Output Handling) — LLM output passed directly to eval(), subprocess, database query without validation. These can be detected in Python (LangChain, OpenAI SDK patterns), TypeScript (Vercel AI SDK, Anthropic SDK patterns), and other languages via regex/AST on import statements + usage patterns. Given the project already has AI-readiness analysis (analyzeAIReadiness), an LlmPromptInjectionRisk and LlmExcessiveAgency biomarker set would naturally extend the existing module. The OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 PDF is the canonical reference (owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications).
evidence: OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 identifies prompt injection as #1 risk. 78% of AI-generated code contains at least one exploitable vulnerability that traditional scanners fail to detect. CVE-2025-53773 (Rules File Backdoor) demonstrates new attack class. LLM-integrated apps have a distinct vulnerability profile not covered by traditional SAST rules.

title: tree-sitter ABI 15 (v0.25+): Supertype API, Reserved Words, and Language Metadata Now Queryable
summary: tree-sitter v0.25.0 (late 2024, stable in 2025) bumped the internal ABI to version 15, embedding language name, version, supertype hierarchies, and reserved words directly into compiled parsers. A new Supertype API exposes subtypes for any supertype symbol, enabling downstream tools to reason about node type relationships (e.g., 'expression' includes 'call_expression', 'binary_expression', etc.). Missing nodes can now be queried. Queries involving supertypes are now validated. This is directly usable in tree-sitter query files: instead of enumerating every concrete expression type in a smell pattern, you can match the supertype 'expression' or 'statement' and get all subtypes automatically. This reduces fragility of existing smell-detection queries and could significantly simplify the GodClass/ComplexMethod query patterns across the project's Tier A languages.
evidence: ABI 15 adds 'the language name, version, supertype info, and reserved words to the parsers.' New function: 'takes in a supertype symbol and returns all associated subtypes.' 'MISSING nodes can now be queried, and queries involving supertypes are properly validated now.' Source: newreleases.io tree-sitter v0.25.0 release notes.

title: tree-sitter v0.26 'Containing Range' QueryCursor API: Scope-Limited Analysis
summary: tree-sitter v0.26 added containing range APIs to QueryCursor. These restrict query results to matches where ALL nodes are fully contained within a given byte or point range, complementing the existing set_byte_range() which returns all intersecting matches. This enables precise function-scope analysis: you can run smell detection queries restricted to the exact byte range of a single function, eliminating false positives from overlapping nodes. For the project's extract-method transformer, this is directly usable to query 'find all deep nesting within this function's byte range' before deciding on a target site, rather than filtering results post-query. Reduces query result set size and improves transformer precision.
evidence: 'v0.26 added containing range APIs to QueryCursor.' The API 'restricts query cursor to only return matches where all nodes are fully contained within the given range, in contrast to set_byte_range().' Source: tree-sitter releases and QueryCursor Rust docs.

title: tree-sitter v0.25 Progress Callback Cancellation: Enables Timeout-Safe Loop Iterations
summary: tree-sitter v0.25 deprecated the old timeout-based cancellation and replaced it with a progress callback that carries error information. Parsing and query operations are now cancelled via the callback rather than a raw timeout integer. For a refactoring loop running dozens of analysis calls per session, this enables the MCP server to implement safe per-call timeouts without killing the Node process — the callback can inspect parse progress and abort gracefully if a single file is taking too long (e.g., minified or generated code). The callback also receives error context, allowing the server to log which specific pattern caused a slow match.
evidence: 'Parsing and Querying should be cancelled using the progress callback, rather than setting a timeout.' Callback now includes error information for precise failure diagnostics. Source: tree-sitter v0.25.0 release notes.

title: tree-sitter Web Bindings Rewritten in TypeScript with CJS+ESM Dual Output (v0.25)
summary: The web-tree-sitter (WASM) JavaScript binding was completely rewritten in TypeScript for v0.25, now publishing both CommonJS and ESM outputs with sourcemaps and debug builds. This directly affects the project's Node.js MCP server: the existing web-tree-sitter dependency can now be imported as a proper ESM module, eliminating the awkward CJS interop shims that are common in older tree-sitter Node integrations. The WASM build also switched from Emscripten to WASI-SDK, with automatic WASI-SDK download on first use via 'tree-sitter build --wasm'. This improves build reproducibility and reduces CI setup complexity.
evidence: v0.25 JavaScript binding: 'Publish both CJS and ESM files,' 'added sourcemaps and debug builds.' WASM: 'Since v0.26.1, tree-sitter build --wasm uses wasi-sdk and will automatically download it on first use.' Source: tree-sitter GitHub releases page.

title: ast-grep: Official MCP Server with Structural Search Across 26+ Languages (No AST Code Required)
summary: The ast-grep project ships an official MCP server (ast-grep/ast-grep-mcp on Docker Hub and crates.io) exposing four tools: dump_syntax_tree, test_match_code_rule, find_code (pattern search), and find_code_by_rule (YAML-rule multi-condition search). Critically, ast-grep's rewrite engine supports automated code transformation via YAML 'fix' rules across all its supported languages (C, C++, Go, Java, Kotlin, Python, Ruby, Rust, TypeScript, TSX, C#, YAML, and more) — not just TS/JS/PHP. For the project, this is the most actionable path to extending automated refactoring beyond the current 3-language limit. The ast-grep-dynamic crate enables runtime loading of additional tree-sitter grammars as shared libraries (.so/.dylib/.dll), meaning new languages can be added without recompiling ast-grep.
evidence: Official MCP server is at github.com/ast-grep/ast-grep-mcp and Docker Hub mcp/ast-grep. Rewrite engine uses YAML 'fix' key with meta-variable substitution, indentation preservation, and FixConfig for surrounding-syntax handling. 'ast-grep-dynamic crate enables runtime loading of custom tree-sitter parsers using libloading... support proprietary or experimental languages without recompilation.' Source: ast-grep official docs and MCP server repo.

title: ast-grep Rewrite Limitation: One Node at a Time — Extract-Method Pattern Requires Workaround
summary: ast-grep's core rewrite engine has a documented hard constraint: 'ast-grep rule can only fix one target node at one time by replacing the target node text with a new string.' This means classic extract-method (which requires simultaneously inserting a new function definition and replacing the original call site) cannot be done in a single ast-grep rule application. However, multi-step transforms are achievable: first apply a rule to add a function-call placeholder, then a second rule to hoist the new function. The project's existing TypeScript/PHP transformers likely already handle this via a two-pass approach. For extending to Go/Python/Rust via ast-grep, this constraint means the auto-refactor output from code_health_auto_refactor would need to decompose transforms into two sequential YAML rules rather than one.
evidence: Direct quote from ast-grep docs: 'ast-grep rule can only fix one target node at one time by replacing the target node text with a new string.' Indentation is preserved automatically. FixConfig with expandStart/expandEnd handles surrounding trivials like commas. Source: ast-grep rewrite-code documentation.

title: Semgrep Autofix: Language-Agnostic Pattern+Fix Rules Including Go, Python, Rust — but Syntax-Level Only
summary: Semgrep's autofix (--autofix flag, 'fix:' YAML key) supports automated code transformation across 30+ languages including Go, Python, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Swift, Elixir, Scala, Ruby, C#, PHP, and more. The 'fix-regex' variant applies regex substitutions to matches. Autofix is syntax-level, not semantic — it cannot perform type-aware or scope-aware transforms, and cross-file rewrites are not supported in autofix (only in pro/paid tiers for dataflow analysis). Cross-function dataflow for Rust was added in 2025. For the project, Semgrep autofix could implement simple smell fixes for DeepNesting (early-return rewrite), MagicNumber (named-constant extraction), and SATD comment removal in any of its 30+ languages, expanding the mechanical-fix rate well beyond the current 11.8%.
evidence: Semgrep supports 'fix:' and 'fix-regex:' keys in rule YAML for all supported languages. 'Reachability coverage for Rust was added [in 2025].' Language list includes Go, Python, Rust, Elixir, Kotlin, Swift, Scala. Official MCP server exists at github.com/semgrep/mcp. Source: semgrep.dev/docs/writing-rules/autofix and supported-languages.

title: GritQL (now Biome/open-source): Declarative Pattern+Transform Language with 200+ Standard Patterns
summary: GritQL is a Rust-based, MIT-licensed query language for structural code search and transformation, built on tree-sitter. Acquired by Honeycomb from Grit.io in April 2025, the GritQL engine itself remains open source under Biome governance. It supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, JSON, Java, Terraform, Solidity, CSS, Markdown, YAML, Rust, Go, and SQL. The stdlib (biomejs/gritql-stdlib) contains 200+ reusable patterns including common upgrade/migration transforms. GritQL's query language uses logic programming constructs (where clauses, not() combinators) that express multi-condition rewrites more naturally than flat YAML. For the project, GritQL's stdlib patterns for Python and Go could directly implement early-return rewriting and God-class splitting — the hardest smells for the project's Tier A non-TS languages.
evidence: GritQL is 'written in Rust for maximum performance and uses tree-sitter for all language parsers.' 'Access to 200+ standard patterns through Grit's built-in module system.' Acquired by Honeycomb in April 2025; 'GritQL, the query engine for codebase analysis and transformation, will remain open source.' Source: Honeycomb blog, biomejs/gritql GitHub, docs.grit.io.

title: Pure-Go Tree-Sitter Runtime (gotreesitter): 206 Grammars, No CGO, Cross-Compile to Any Platform
summary: The gotreesitter library is a ground-up reimplementation of the tree-sitter runtime in pure Go with no CGO and no C toolchain dependency. It ships 206 embedded grammars as compressed binary blobs (lazy-loaded on first use). Single-file parsing is sub-millisecond; 66 Go files parse in 83ms, 1,131 Python files in 400ms, 300 Rust files in 300ms. Binary size increases from ~12MB to ~32MB due to embedded grammar data. For the project: this approach is irrelevant for the Node.js MCP server, but if a future Go-based CLI tool or sidecar were built (e.g., for git-history analysis using Go's go-git), gotreesitter eliminates all C-toolchain CI setup issues. Also signals that the tree-sitter grammar ecosystem is mature enough that 206 grammars can be embedded into a single binary.
evidence: gotreesitter: 'a ground-up reimplementation of the tree-sitter runtime in pure Go... 205 embedded grammars as compressed blobs.' Benchmarks: 66 Go files in 83ms, FastAPI (1,131 files) in 400ms, Axum (300 Rust files) in 300ms. Source: dev.to article by thegdsks, 2025.

title: Tree-Sitter Knowledge Graph via MCP: 10x Token Reduction for Structural Queries
summary: A March 2026 arxiv paper (2603.27277) demonstrates that pre-building a persistent tree-sitter-based knowledge graph (parsed across 66 languages) and exposing it via MCP achieves 10x fewer tokens and 2.1x fewer tool calls compared to file-exploration agents, while maintaining 83% answer quality (vs 92% for full exploration). The system uses parallel worker pools, call-graph traversal, and community detection. For the project, this suggests that the refactoring loop's token cost could be dramatically reduced by replacing repeated code_health_review calls (which re-read and re-analyze full files) with a pre-built structural index. A cached AST knowledge graph that the AI queries for smell locations would use far fewer tokens than repeatedly sending full file contents.
evidence: Paper 2603.27277: 'ten times fewer tokens' and '2.1 times fewer tool calls' vs file-exploration agents. Parses 66 languages. 'Matches or exceeds the explorer on 19 of 31 languages' for graph-native queries. Source: arxiv.org/abs/2603.27277, March 2026.

title: JCodeMunch: Tree-Sitter MCP Server Reporting 5-5.5x Token Reduction via AST Index-Once Query
summary: JCodeMunch (github.com/jgravelle/jcodemunch-mcp) is a token-efficient MCP server for GitHub source code exploration using tree-sitter AST parsing. It reports roughly 80% fewer tokens (5x efficiency) vs file-content sharing, with specific examples showing 3,850 tokens reduced to 700 (5.5x). The model is: index the AST once per session, then answer structural queries cheaply. For the project's refactoring loop: instead of the AI receiving full file text in code_health_review responses, the MCP server could return only the relevant AST node offsets and the specific smell locations. The AI then requests targeted excerpts via focusLines rather than full file content. This could be layered on top of the existing MCP tools without replacing them.
evidence: 'roughly 80% fewer tokens, or 5x more efficient — index once, query cheaply forever.' Specific example: '3,850 tokens reduced to just 700 — a 5.5x improvement.' Source: github.com/jgravelle/jcodemunch-mcp README.

title: Python rope library: mature, programmatic extract-method API ready for MCP integration
summary: Rope (python-rope/rope) is a pure-Python refactoring library that exposes ExtractMethod and ExtractVariable via a typed offset-based API. You pass a Project, a Resource file object, and integer start/end byte offsets; get_changes('new_name') returns a Change object you apply with project.do(changes). It supports Python 3.8-3.13, handles project-wide rename propagation, and is already wrapped in an MCP server on mcpmarket.com ("Rope: Python Refactoring for Claude & CLI"). Crucially: no IDE dependency, fully headless, subprocess-safe. This is the most direct path to adding Python automated extract-method to the Healthy AI Code MCP server with minimal friction. The limitation is that rope does not automatically decide WHICH code block to extract — that selection logic must come from the health scorer (ComplexMethod/BrainMethod smell pointing to a function + a specific range), making it a perfect fit for an MCP-driven loop: the smell detector finds the target, the LLM proposes the range offsets, rope executes the extraction.
evidence: rope.readthedocs.io documents ExtractVariable/ExtractMethod with exact constructor signature (project, resource, start_offset, end_offset) and get_changes() API. mcpmarket.com confirms an existing MCP server wrapping rope is already shipped.

title: gopls CLI: headless Go extract-function and extract-method via codeaction -exec
summary: gopls (the official Go language server) ships refactor.extract.function, refactor.extract.method, refactor.extract.variable, and refactor.extract.constant as non-interactive code actions accessible through the CLI: `gopls codeaction -exec -kind refactor.extract.function -diff file.go:#start-#end`. The v0.17.0 release (2024-2025) also added refactor.extract.toNewFile and multiple bug fixes to extract/inline operations. The key insight for the MCP use case: gopls codeaction is fully non-interactive and produces a unified diff on stdout — it does not require VS Code or any GUI. Integration pattern: health scorer detects a ComplexMethod smell in a Go file at a specific function body range, the LLM resolves byte offsets, the MCP tool shells out to gopls and applies the diff. Known gaps: comment stripping during extract/inline (issue #20744), and some complex control-flow cases (issues #66289, #63394). These are known regressions, not blockers.
evidence: go.dev/gopls/features/transformation documents the full CLI syntax and lists all 12 refactor.extract.* and refactor.rewrite.* code actions with before/after examples. v0.17.0 release notes confirm 2024-2025 improvements to extract robustness.

title: REM2.0: headless Rust extract-function daemon, but VSCode coupling limits MCP use
summary: REM2.0 (arXiv:2601.19207, January 2026) is a daemon-based extract-function toolchain for Rust built atop rust-analyzer. It reduces extraction latency from ~1000ms to single-digit milliseconds and adds a repairer that automatically fixes lifetime and borrow-checker errors introduced by extraction. It handles async/await, generics, const fn, non-local control flow, and higher-ranked trait bounds — the full real-world Rust surface. On the original 40-case corpus it achieves 100% compatibility. The critical limitation for the project: REM2.0 is designed with a VSCode front-end and currently has no documented standalone CLI or programmatic API usable from an external process like an MCP server. However, since it runs as a persistent rust-analyzer daemon, there is a viable (medium-effort) path to integrating it via a thin LSP client that sends textDocument/codeAction requests to the daemon process — the same mechanism gopls uses. This would give Rust safe extract-function with borrow-checker awareness, a capability no other tool currently provides without IDE dependency.
evidence: arXiv:2601.19207 (January 2026): '100% compatibility on the original 40-case REM corpus; extends to async/await, generics, non-local control flow, and higher-ranked trait bounds. Latency reduced from ~1000ms to single-digit ms inside daemon.' VSCode-only front-end is an explicit architectural constraint in the paper.

title: ast-grep: polyglot AST-based rewriter covering 26+ languages including Python, Go, Ruby, Rust, Elixir
summary: ast-grep (written in Rust, multi-threaded) supports pattern-match-and-rewrite rules authored in YAML across C, C++, Go, Python, Ruby, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Elixir, Swift, Scala, and 15 more languages — all using tree-sitter grammars. Its fix/rewrite mechanism applies structural rewrites without requiring full language-server infrastructure. The critical distinction: ast-grep excels at pattern-based rewrites (rename, change call signature, swap idioms) but cannot perform extract-method semantically because extract-method requires inserting a new top-level function definition and updating the call site simultaneously — a two-location edit that ast-grep's rewriter rules do not natively support. However, ast-grep CAN mechanically perform early-return/guard-clause conversion (DeepNesting reduction) by matching `if (cond) { ... long body ... }` at a function's top level and rewriting to `if (!cond) return; ... body ...`. This class of single-location, same-scope rewrites is exactly what DeepNesting and some BrainMethod cases need. A jssg (JavaScript ast-grep) wrapper from codemod.com provides a typed TS authoring model for this engine.
evidence: ast-grep.github.io/reference/yaml documents supported languages list (26 including all Tier A languages). ast-grep.github.io/guide/rewrite-code shows fix: key pattern for structural rewrite. Tool comparison page confirms multi-threaded Rust engine. codemod.com/blog/jssg announces jssg as typed TS wrapper.

title: OpenRewrite: 5000+ Java/Kotlin recipes via LST, no extract-method recipe but style/complexity recipes exist
summary: OpenRewrite (Moderne, Apache-licensed) builds a Lossless Semantic Tree (LST) — a compiler-accurate, type-resolved representation — and applies imperative or declarative recipes to it safely. The 5000+ recipe catalog covers Java, Kotlin, Groovy, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, and C#. Critically: there is NO native extract-method recipe. OpenRewrite is designed for mechanical API-level changes (rename, migrate framework, fix import, change method signature) rather than complexity-driven decomposition. Where it IS useful for the project: (1) Java/Kotlin early-return/guard-clause recipes CAN be authored using OpenRewrite's MethodMatcher + JavaTemplate visitor pattern; (2) OpenRewrite's Maven/Gradle plugin integration makes it trivially runnable in a subprocess by an MCP tool; (3) A custom ComplexMethod→early-return recipe for Java/Kotlin would be a high-value addition, covering the project's largest untransformed language pair. The effort to build such a recipe is medium: ~200 lines of Java using JavaVisitor + complexity analysis from the project's existing tree-sitter detectors.
evidence: docs.openrewrite.org confirms LST approach and 5000+ recipes. Java category page lists no extract-method or complexity-reduction recipe. Writing-a-Java-refactoring-recipe guide shows JavaVisitor + JavaTemplate API used for imperative transformations. cronn.de/en/java/2025/10/23/openrewrite-for-refactoring documents industrial use in 2025.

title: MANTRA: LLM multi-agent extract-method framework achieving 82.8% test-pass rate for Java
summary: MANTRA (arXiv:2503.14340, March 2025) combines context-aware RAG, multi-agent LLM collaboration, and verbal reinforcement learning for method-level refactoring. On 703 Java refactoring instances across 10 projects, it achieves 82.8% compilation+test-pass success rate vs 8.7% for raw GPT baseline — a 9.5x improvement. It also shows 50% improvement in Extract Method quality over IntelliJ's EM-Assist. The architecture is relevant to this project's loop design: (1) the RAG component retrieves similar previously-refactored code snippets as few-shot examples before asking the LLM to propose the extraction — this is directly applicable to the MCP's followUpInstruction field; (2) verbal reinforcement learning means the LLM receives structured textual feedback about test failures and revises, which mirrors the project's score-based loop but adds a compilation/test-pass gate before scoring. The limitation: MANTRA is Java-only in evaluation and requires a test suite to validate success. Adding a compilation check (javac) before health rescoring would approximate MANTRA's safety guarantee.
evidence: arXiv:2503.14340v2: '82.8% success rate (582/703) producing code that compiles and passes all tests vs 8.7% raw GPT baseline; 50% improvement vs EM-Assist on Extract Method.' RAG + verbal RL methodology described in full.

title: RCI prompting: 83% test-pass rate for LLM extract-method on Python (open-source models)
summary: arXiv:2510.26480 (October 2025) evaluated five open-source LLMs (3B–8B params) on extract-method refactoring for Python code. Recursive Criticism and Improvement (RCI) prompting — where the model critiques its own output and iteratively revises — achieves 82.9% test-pass rate (Deepseek-Coder-RCI) and 80.8% (Qwen2.5-Coder-RCI), with over 70% developer acceptance in user studies. One-shot prompting achieved significantly lower rates. The direct implication: the project's followUpInstruction field in code_health_auto_refactor should include an RCI-style self-critique prompt alongside the structured refactoring steps. Specifically: after proposing extracted code, the LLM should be asked to verify (a) all free variables are passed as parameters, (b) return values are correctly handled, (c) the original call site compiles. This is a low-effort change to the MCP's instruction generation that could materially improve the 20% single-pass fix rate.
evidence: arXiv:2510.26480: 'Deepseek-Coder-RCI and Qwen2.5-Coder-RCI achieve TPP scores of 0.829 and 0.808. RCI-based prompting consistently outperforms one-shot prompting in test pass rates and refactoring quality.'

title: PolyglotPiranha (Uber): tree-sitter-based rule-driven transformer for 10 languages, proven at industrial scale
summary: PolyglotPiranha (uber/piranha, PLDI 2024) is a rule-driven code transformation engine using tree-sitter grammars that supports Java, Kotlin, Swift, Go, Python, Scala, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Thrift. It was deployed industrially at Uber: 210K lines of dead code deleted and 20K lines migrated across 1,611 pull requests. Rules are expressed as tree-sitter query patterns with replacement actions, similar to ast-grep but with cascading/chained rule support. This cascading capability is the key differentiator: a Piranha rule can trigger follow-on rules (e.g., remove now-unreachable imports after dead code removal), which maps well to the smell cascade problem (fixing GodClass may expose DeadCode, which exposes unused imports). For the project's Go, Python, Kotlin, Scala, and Swift Tier A languages, Piranha provides an industrial-grade, headless, subprocess-callable transformer that doesn't require language server infrastructure. The limitation vs rope or gopls: it handles mechanical rule-based rewrites well but not semantic extract-method (same constraint as ast-grep).
evidence: PLDI 2024 paper and uber/piranha GitHub README: 'Deleted 210K lines of dead code and migrated 20K lines across 1611 pull requests. Supports Java, Kotlin, Swift, Go, Python, Scala, JavaScript, TypeScript, Thrift via tree-sitter.' pypi.org/project/polyglot-piranha confirms pip-installable headless tool.

title: GritQL: Rust-powered declarative pattern-rewrite language over tree-sitter, 26+ languages including all Tier A
summary: GritQL (biomejs/gritql, now embedded in Biome and available standalone) is a declarative query language for code search and rewriting backed by tree-sitter and implemented in Rust. It supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, JSON, Terraform, Solidity, CSS, Markdown, YAML, Rust, Go, SQL, and more (26+ total). The authoring model is simpler than ast-grep YAML: pattern queries use backtick code templates with $metavariable holes and => for the replacement, similar to comby but with full tree-sitter AST awareness. GritQL scales to 10M+ line repos and is substantially faster than Semgrep at repo-scan scale. For the project: GritQL rules can mechanically convert `if (complex_condition) { large_body }` patterns to guard-clause/early-return form across all supported Tier A languages in a single tool invocation. A library of such rules (one per smell type, per language) would extend the mechanical fix capability beyond TS/JS/PHP with low authoring overhead. The catch: like ast-grep and Piranha, GritQL cannot semantically extract-method (it can pattern-match a function body but cannot generate a new top-level function in the same operation).
evidence: docs.grit.io lists 26+ supported languages. biomejs/gritql GitHub README confirms Rust implementation, tree-sitter backend, and declarative => rewrite syntax. DEV Community post by herrington_darkholme benchmarks GritQL vs ast-grep for JS/TS transformations (2025).

title: tree-sitter cannot mutate AST in-place: write-back requires source-text manipulation, not AST serialization
summary: A critical architectural constraint confirmed by tree-sitter maintainers (GitHub discussions #642, #1085, #2553): tree-sitter has no API for mutating a parsed tree and serializing it back to source text. The only pattern is (1) parse → (2) identify ranges in source text → (3) edit source text directly as a string → (4) re-parse the modified text (using the old tree as a hint for incremental parsing, which is much faster). This means the project's existing approach of passing code strings and asking the LLM to return modified strings is architecturally sound and aligns with tree-sitter's design. Any automated transformer (rope, gopls, GritQL, ast-grep) must operate on the source text level, not the AST level. This validates the MCP design but also explains why building a generic 'AST mutation' layer on top of tree-sitter would be wrong — each language needs a tool that understands source-text implications of AST changes (scoping, imports, formatting).
evidence: tree-sitter/tree-sitter Discussion #1108 ('Suitability for automated code refactoring'): 'tree-sitter doesn't have APIs for mutating syntax trees and then reflecting those changes back as text diffs. That's something you'd need to build yourself.' GitHub issue #642 confirms this is by design.

title: False Positives and Alert Fatigue Are the Primary Adoption Killers
summary: FSE 2025 empirical study found that 50.8% of all static analysis warning suppressions have no effect on any warning — developers are suppressing noise that doesn't even exist. False positive rates range from 18% to 86% depending on the tool. The SAST+LLM post-processing combination reduced false positives by 91% over standalone Semgrep. Teams that deploy too many blocking checks at once trigger alert fatigue within two weeks, eroding developer trust permanently. An LLM-driven adaptive approach reduced average triage time by 31% and improved user-reported trust in alerts; removing false positive filtering increases FPR by 39%.
evidence: FSE 2025: 50.8% of suppressions affect no warning. LLM+SAST study: 91% FP reduction vs standalone Semgrep (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3773365.3773410). Alert fatigue observed within 2 weeks of over-aggressive blocking gates.

title: The 'Clean as You Code' / New-Code-Only Gate Strategy Drives Adoption Without Legacy Paralysis
summary: SonarSource's incremental analysis on SonarQube 2025.x skips unchanged files entirely for languages like CSS, Go, Ruby, Scala (full skip) and caches previous results for Java, JS, C#, Python. The 'New Code Period' pattern — gate enforcement only on code written since last version or last X days — is now the dominant enterprise adoption strategy. Teams start with gates set to pass 80% of existing code, then tighten thresholds 5% per month. This prevents the 'import a legacy project and drown in 10,000 findings' failure mode that kills adoption. ArXiv research confirms writing clean new code reduces Technical Debt Density faster than big-bang remediation.
evidence: SonarQube 2025.1 docs: unchanged files skipped for Go, Ruby, Scala; cache reused for Java/JS/C#. ArXiv 2010.09161: clean new code strategy reduces TD density. Enterprise pattern: baseline at 80%, tighten 5%/month.

title: GitHub's Organization-Level Code Quality Dashboard (Oct 2025) Defines the New Baseline for PR-Native Integration
summary: GitHub Code Quality went public preview in October 2025, with an org-level dashboard added in February 2026. It provides reliability and maintainability scores surfaced inline in PRs as CodeQL-backed findings, with one-click Copilot-powered autofixes. Key DX drivers: one-click enablement, in-PR timing (findings appear when developer is already reviewing), and batched autofix for entire classes of issues. The frictionless setup combined with PR-native delivery is the pattern that drives stickiness. This is now what developers expect as a baseline from any code quality tool — PR-inline findings, an org dashboard, and one-click fix.
evidence: GitHub Changelog Oct 2025: one-click enablement, inline PR findings, Copilot autofix. Feb 2026: org-level dashboard with per-repo reliability/maintainability scores. Competitor offering zero-friction entry at the PR layer.

title: GitHub Copilot Code Review: 71% Actionability Rate and Multi-Line Clustering Are the New Precision Benchmarks
summary: GitHub Copilot Code Review reached 60 million reviews by May 2026 (10x growth since April 2025 GA). Key quality signals: 71% of reviews surface actionable feedback; the remaining 29% produce no comments ('silence is better than noise'). Average 5.1 comments per review. Multi-line comments attached to logical code ranges (not single lines) and clustering of similar pattern errors into cohesive units drove an 8.1% increase in positive feedback. Batch autofixes resolve entire classes of issues at once. Developer case study: WEX saw 30% more code shipped after making Copilot review default. These are the precision/recall benchmarks the market now judges code review tools against.
evidence: GitHub Blog: 71% actionability, 5.1 avg comments, 8.1% positive feedback gain from multi-line clustering, batch autofix, 60M reviews. WEX: 30% more code shipped. 12,000+ orgs run on every PR.

title: VS Code MCP Support Is Generally Available (July 2025) — Native IDE Distribution Channel Now Open
summary: VS Code MCP support moved from preview to GA in July 2025 (VS Code 1.102+). MCP servers can be bundled inside VS Code extensions, run as stdio child processes (no port management, lifecycle tied to extension), and are auto-available on extension install. BifrostMCP demonstrates the pattern: a VS Code extension exposing LSP-backed semantic tools (find usages, rename, type info, code actions) via MCP to AI assistants. The VS Code AI Toolkit also gained a Tool Catalog in March 2026 for building/testing MCP servers directly. This creates a zero-friction distribution channel: ship a VS Code extension, get MCP tools automatically, no separate server setup.
evidence: GitHub Changelog July 2025: MCP GA in VS Code 1.102. VS Code Extension API docs: stdio transport, extension-bundled MCP servers. BifrostMCP on GitHub: LSP tools via MCP. VS Mag March 2026: AI Toolkit Tool Catalog.

title: CodeScene's 'Biomarker + Hotspot' Model Drives Stakeholder Buy-In Through Multi-Channel Visibility
summary: CodeScene uses a 1-10 health score (same scale as this project) backed by ~25-30 biomarkers validated against defect density. Their key DX insight: top hotspots are only a minor fraction of code but account for 25-70% of resolved defects — scoping feedback to hotspots rather than whole-codebase noise dramatically improves signal quality. Adoption is driven by multi-channel presentation: visual health trends over time, architectural monitoring for microservices, CI/CD PR checks, README status badges, and stakeholder-readable dashboards. The medical analogy ('biomarker' vs 'code smell') is also a deliberate DX choice to avoid absolutist language and position the tool as 'a friendly, unbiased team member'.
evidence: CodeScene docs: 25-30 biomarkers, 1-10 scale, hotspots = 25-70% of defects. Multi-channel: trends, arch monitoring, CI, README badges. Language: 'biomarker' framing vs 'smell' to reduce developer defensiveness.

title: Blocking vs. Advisory Mode: Blocking Gates Without Emergency Bypass Procedures Kill Hotfix Velocity
summary: Industry guidance has consolidated around a two-mode approach: hard-blocking gates for security/critical issues (0 new blockers, 0 new vulnerabilities), advisory/warning mode for quality smells and maintainability issues. Blocking gates create a documented failure mode during production incidents — they block urgent hotfixes. Best practice now requires documented emergency bypass procedures plus post-incident security review. The 'incremental + new code only' pattern combined with non-blocking advisory comments for quality issues maximizes adoption without sacrificing standards. Augment Code's 2025 enterprise guide cites 40% velocity improvement from proper gate configuration (advisory for most, hard-block only for critical issues).
evidence: Multiple 2025 enterprise guides: hard-block only critical/security, advisory for quality. Emergency bypass requirement for hotfixes. Augment Code: 40% velocity improvement claim from proper gate configuration.

title: AI Code Churn Rate as Leading Quality Signal — Elite Teams Track AI-Written Code Separately
summary: The 2026 developer productivity research from Zylos identifies 'AI code churn rate' — what fraction of recently AI-generated code is deleted or rewritten within 30 days — as a key leading quality indicator that DORA misses. AI now writes 41% of all code (SonarSource State of Code 2026), code duplication increased 4x with AI, and delivery stability decreased 7.2%. Elite teams segment PRs by AI vs. human authorship and track churn differently for each. For a code health MCP server, this creates an opportunity: expose AI-churn detection as a distinct biomarker, correlating recent large AI-generated additions with subsequent rewrites from git history.
evidence: Zylos 2026: AI churn = 'hidden quality signal'. SonarSource State of Code 2026: 41% AI-written, 4x duplication increase, 7.2% stability decrease. DORA 2025 report confirms AI as multiplier that exposes team weaknesses.

title: DeepSource AST-Based Autofix Pipeline: The Pattern for Reliable Mechanical Fixes
summary: DeepSource's Autofix (exits beta Feb 2026) operates on ASTs rather than raw text to ensure structural correctness regardless of formatting. Multi-stage pipeline: detection via 5,000+ rules on AST, transformation on AST, syntactic validation, then PR diff presentation. Developers review diffs before applying — no auto-merge. The AST-first approach matches what this project's TS/JS/PHP transformers do, validating the architectural choice. Key DX finding: fixes presented as 'reviewable diffs in PR comments with single-click application' is the adoption-maximizing pattern. Batch 'Fix All' for entire smell categories (added April 2026) is now expected by developers.
evidence: DeepSource 2026: AST-first transformation, 5,000+ rules, syntactic validation before presentation. Cursor BugBot 'Fix All' April 2026. Pattern: reviewable diff + single-click = adoption-maximizing workflow.

title: SonarQube IDE Extension Now Supports Claude Code and Cursor — Real-Time Health Feedback Becomes Expected
summary: SonarQube for IDE (free extension) now lists Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, and IntelliJ as supported environments, providing real-time feedback as you type. Anthropic shipped native LSP support for Claude Code in December 2025 (v2.0.74) with automatic diagnostics after every file edit. This means the market expectation has shifted: code health feedback should be available as real-time IDE diagnostics, not just at CI time. The LSP/IDE layer is now a required distribution channel for developer-facing code quality tools, not an optional enhancement.
evidence: SonarSource product page: Claude Code listed as supported IDE. Amir Teymoori blog: 'LSP integration is the difference between an AI that guesses and one that knows'. Claude Code v2.0.74 (Dec 2025): native LSP with post-edit diagnostics.

title: Developer Trust Calibration: Explain WHY, Not Just WHAT — Warning Messages as Adoption Lever
summary: Research consensus across multiple 2025 studies: warning messages that explain why a pattern is harmful (business impact, defect risk, maintenance cost) dramatically improve developer trust and action rates vs. messages that only name the violation. GitHub Copilot's positive feedback improvement came partly from adding reasoning context to comments. SonarQube for IDE 'explains why each issue is harmful and shows how to fix it'. This is an actionable DX differentiator: each MCP tool response should include a 1-2 sentence 'why this hurts' explanation tied to concrete outcomes (defect risk, review time, onboarding cost), not just the smell name and fix.
evidence: incident.io 2025: explaining WHY reduces alert fatigue. GitHub Copilot: reasoning context drove 8.1% + 6% positive feedback gains. SonarQube IDE: 'explains why each issue is harmful'. Reduces suppression rate by improving developer understanding of risk.

title: Structural Erosion Index: A Validated Complexity-Mass Biomarker for Agentic Degradation
summary: SlopCodeBench (arxiv 2603.24755, March 2026) formally defines and validates a 'structural erosion' metric: Erosion = Σ(mass in high-CC functions) / Σ(all mass), where mass(f) = CC(f) × √SLOC(f), and 'high-CC' means CC > 10. Across 11 AI coding agents, erosion increased in 80% of trajectories; mean high-CC function count grew from 4.1 to 37.0 across checkpoints; maximum CC climbed from 27.1 to 68.2. Agent code showed 0.68±0.20 erosion vs 0.31±0.17 for human-written baselines (2.2× worse). This metric captures something distinct from raw cyclomatic complexity: it measures how much of a file's total 'complexity mass' is concentrated in already-complex functions, detecting the snowball effect. The project's current ComplexMethod and BrainMethod biomarkers do not capture this distribution/concentration property. Adding a 'ComplexityMassConcentration' smell (fires when erosion > 0.60 for a file) would give the loop a signal specifically tuned to agentic degradation patterns.
evidence: 80% of agentic trajectories showed rising erosion; human baseline erosion 0.31 vs agent 0.68; validated across 11 models on 36 problems

title: Verbosity / Structural Duplication as a Temporal Smell (Separate from DeadCode)
summary: SlopCodeBench tracked a 'verbosity' metric (fraction of redundant/duplicated code) using AST-Grep rules (137 patterns) plus clone detection, normalized to [0,1]. Verbosity increased in 89.8% of agent trajectories, with agent repos showing 0.32±0.11 vs 0.11±0.07 for human code — a 3× gap. Structural duplication specifically drove 66% of verbosity growth in 72.1% of trajectories. The current project has a DuplicateCode smell, but it appears to be static-analysis-only. Adding a TEMPORAL verbosity signal — tracking how much the fraction of duplicated code has grown since the previous commit batch — would identify files in a 'duplication growth spiral' and deprioritize them for automated refactoring (since guided agents do better on them when they are flagged early). This is distinct from a point-in-time DuplicateCode count.
evidence: 89.8% of agentic trajectories showed rising verbosity; 3× gap between agent and human-written code; driven by structural duplication in 72.1% of cases

title: Bumpy Road: Multi-Chunk Nested Logic as a Cognitive-Load Biomarker
summary: CodeScene's 'Bumpy Road' code smell (September 2025 blog post) measures not total cyclomatic complexity but the DISTRIBUTION of nested conditional logic within a function: (1) number of discrete 'bumps' (separate blocks of nested conditions), (2) nesting depth per bump, (3) size/span of each bump in lines. The intuition is that working memory can hold 3-4 items, and each additional bump is a separate context-switch. A function with CC=15 from one large nested block is harder to refactor but easier to mentally hold than one with CC=6 distributed across 4 separate nested chunks. The project currently has DeepNesting (nesting depth) and ComplexMethod (raw CC), but not the distribution/chunk-count dimension. Adding a 'BumpyRoad' smell — fires when a function contains ≥3 nested conditional chunks with mean depth ≥2 — is implementable via tree-sitter by counting top-level conditional blocks within a function body, each of which contains nested conditionals.
evidence: CodeScene validates this across 'hundreds of codebases'; grounded in cognitive psychology research on working memory limits (3-4 items). No single-number complexity metric captures multi-chunk distribution.

title: Line-Level Hotspot Patterns: 15 Recurring Outlier Classes with Bot Contamination Filter
summary: A February 2026 arxiv paper (2602.13170) analyzed 3.27M files and found only 0.87% contain hotspot lines (outliers at μ+3σ modifications or >1 change/project-month). 15 recurring pattern classes were identified: Pinned Version Bump (26%), Long Line Change (17%), Formatting Ping-Pong (9%), plus configuration management, dev-env settings, and license patterns. Crucially, 74% of hotspot edits were by automated bots (23 unique bots identified), with 95% of Metadata Changes and 52% of Pinned Version Bumps being bot-authored. For the project's hotspot analysis, this implies two concrete improvements: (1) filter bot-authored commits from churn calculations (currently likely conflating bot churn with human churn, inflating hotspot scores incorrectly); (2) classify hotspot types — a 'FormatPingPong' smell can be detected when a file's diff shows alternating style-only changes (detectable via AST-equivalent change with zero semantic delta). Median hotspot lifespan was 3.28 years with a maximum of 18.1 years.
evidence: 3.27M files analyzed; 74% of hotspot edits were bot-generated; 15 pattern classes validated; median 11 edits per hotspot; median 3.28-year lifespan

title: MCP-Guided Agentic Refactoring Achieves 2-5x Better Code Health vs Unguided
summary: CodeScene's March 2026 benchmark directly compared raw Claude Code vs CodeHealth MCP-guided Claude Code on a 25,000-file dataset. The MCP-guided approach achieved 2-5x more Code Health improvements. Most importantly: unguided agents performed 54,094 rename-variable operations vs 21,702 extract-method; guided agents flipped this to 21,702 extract-methods vs 8,640 renames — a 2.9x shift toward structural refactorings and 84% reduction in shallow cosmetic changes. The MCP-guided agent received 'complexity drivers, readability issues, excessive responsibilities, and structural smells' as concrete actionable feedback. This directly validates the project's current tool design. The implication for token reduction: the project should ensure its `followUpInstruction` output is maximally specific about WHICH function to extract and WHY (naming the exact nesting pattern or bump), since this specificity is what guides the agent away from rename-variable noise.
evidence: 2-5x more Code Health improvement with MCP guidance; 2.9x more structural refactorings; 84% fewer cosmetic renames; validated on 25K-file dataset

title: Code Health Threshold 9.4 for AI-Reliability: Validated Against Bug Introduction Rate
summary: CodeScene's research (referenced in March 2026 benchmark post) found that AI-induced bugs are reliably avoided when Code Health reaches ≥9.4 — closely matching the project's own 9.5 threshold but providing independent empirical validation from a different methodology. The average hotspot Code Health in the IT sector is 5.15, and the human-readability threshold is 9.0. The narrow band 9.0-9.5 is where code is 'human-maintainable but AI-unreliable'. This validates the project's threshold choice, but suggests an intermediate threshold (~9.2) could be exposed as a named tier: 'AIAssisted' (human can work, AI needs supervision). No change needed, but this evidence strengthens the case for the 9.5 AI_READY_THRESHOLD in conversations with operators building on top of the MCP.
evidence: AI-induced bugs reliably avoided at Code Health ≥9.4; industry average hotspot health is 5.15; human threshold 9.0; validated from independent dataset

title: Function-Level Change Coupling as a Third Tier Beyond File-Level Coupling
summary: CodeScene documents change coupling at three levels: architectural, file, and function level. The project's current MethodTemporalCoupling detects methods that co-change within a file's git history. What is not yet implemented is CROSS-FILE function-level coupling: detecting when function A in file X and function B in file Y consistently co-change within the same commit. This is architecturally more expensive to compute (requires cross-file method range attribution) but gives far higher signal precision — a file-level coupling between two large files may be caused by one specific function pair, not the whole file. The threshold parameters from CodeScene docs are informative: minimum 10 revisions, minimum 10 shared commits, minimum 50% coupling strength. A new tool `code_health_cross_file_coupling` returning method pairs with coupling strength, shared-commit count, and suggested co-location or interface extraction would directly address hidden architectural dependencies not visible from static analysis.
evidence: CodeScene operates at 3 levels; current project only has within-file method temporal coupling; cross-file function coupling requires building a commit-indexed function range map across all files

title: Knowledge Island Detection: File-Importance-Weighted Bus Factor
summary: The 'Knowledge Islands' tool (arxiv 2408.08733, 2024) and BFSig paper (ACM ESEC/FSE 2023) both found that standard bus factor calculations — counting the minimum set of developers who authored >50% of files — are distorted when all files are treated as equal. BFSig weights files by significance (complexity × change frequency = hotspot weight) before computing the bus factor. This means a 10,000-line god class has higher significance than a 50-line utility file. The project's current KnowledgeLoss biomarker is already computing something in this space, but a more precise implementation would: (1) compute per-file ownership concentration (Gini coefficient of authorship by lines/commits), (2) weight by the file's complexity-churn product (its hotspot score), (3) fire a 'KnowledgeIsland' smell when file hotspot score >7 AND single-author attribution >70%. This would pinpoint high-risk silos rather than just high-risk general knowledge loss.
evidence: BFSig paper validated that file-significance weighting improves bus factor estimation; knowledge-island tool found to identify high-impact single-author files with Truck Factor calculations

title: Microservice Logical Coupling: Cross-Repo Change Coupling as Architecture Smell
summary: Research (Springer 2025, ScienceDirect 2023) formalizes 'microservice logical coupling': two microservices are logically coupled when files from both are modified in the same commit. CodeScene documents this works across git repository boundaries. For the project, this represents an extension to the existing `analyzeFileCoupling` function: currently it likely operates within a single repository. A new tool `code_health_cross_repo_coupling` could accept a list of repository paths, identify commits touching multiple repos (via timestamp+author fingerprint if not a monorepo), and report inter-service coupling strength. This is a moat feature — no other code-health MCP currently surfaces this. It directly addresses microservice teams who want to know if their 'independent' services are actually coupled in practice. Key threshold: couples with <10 shared commits or <30% coupling strength should be filtered as noise.
evidence: 2025 empirical study on microservice ownership; CodeScene cross-repo analysis documented; no competing code-health MCP implements this

title: Unhealthy Code Consumes Significantly More AI Tokens: Direct Causal Data
summary: CodeScene's May 2026 blog post ('Unhealthy code is burning your token usage — here's the data') provides empirical evidence that low Code Health directly increases token consumption in AI-assisted development. While the detailed numbers were not accessible (404 on direct fetch), the title and surrounding context from the agentic benchmarks reference '~50% lower token consumption for comparable tasks' on uplifted codebases. This is the quantitative argument for prioritizing code health improvement BEFORE running AI coding agents on a codebase. For the project's marketing/strategic positioning, this means adding a new MCP tool: `code_health_token_forecast` that estimates the expected token cost of an AI coding session based on current Code Health scores (lower health = higher forecast), giving operators a business-case metric alongside the health score itself.
evidence: CodeScene May 2026 post reports data correlation between code health and token usage; benchmark post references ~50% token reduction at uplifted code health; independent motivation for the project's core value proposition

title: LM-CC: A New LLM-Perceived Complexity Metric That Outperforms Cyclomatic and Cognitive Complexity
