summary: A February 2026 paper introduces LM-CC, decomposing code into entropy-based semantic units organized in a compositional hierarchy. LM-CC = 0.8·TotalBranch + 0.2·TotalCompLevel. It achieves partial correlations of r=-0.93 (program repair), r=-0.97 (code translation), r=-0.92 (execution reasoning) with LLM task performance — far exceeding traditional metrics whose correlations disappear after controlling for code length. Crucially, rewriting code to reduce LM-CC while holding cyclomatic complexity constant improves LLM program-repair by +20.9% and code translation by +10.2%. Traditional cyclomatic complexity, Halstead, and cognitive complexity all lose predictive power after length control. The key driver: deeply nested conditionals produce O(n²) LM-CC versus O(n) for flat equivalents with identical cyclomatic complexity. Implementation uses token-level entropy from a pretrained model (CodeLlama-7b) with threshold τ=0.67 (67th percentile of token entropies), plus syntactic boundary detection. This is a viable new biomarker for 'LLM Refactorability' in the Healthy AI Code MCP.
evidence: Partial correlations r=-0.93 to -0.97 with LLM task performance; +20.9% program repair improvement from LM-CC reduction; formula LM-CC = 0.8·TotalBranch + 0.2·TotalCompLevel verified from full paper fetch.

title: SonarSource 2025.1: Nested Function Cognitive Complexity No Longer Adds to Parent in JS/TS
summary: SonarQube 2025.1 LTA changed cognitive complexity calculation for JavaScript and TypeScript: nested function complexity is no longer aggregated to the parent function's score. Each function is now scored independently. This will cause measured cognitive complexity to drop for any TS/JS code using callbacks, arrow functions, or closures. The Healthy AI Code MCP project computes ComplexMethod via its own tree-sitter implementation. If it uses the old (pre-2025.1) nested-function-aggregation approach, its scoring is now diverged from the industry standard. This is worth auditing and potentially aligning. The official SonarSource threshold is ≤15 for most languages, ≤25 for C/C++/Objective-C. Empirical validation confirms cognitive complexity is correlated with defects and understandability at a statistically significant level, though its predictive advantage over traditional cyclomatic complexity is modest — the two are nearly co-linear after controlling for method size.
evidence: Official SonarQube 2025.1 release notes confirm nested function complexity no longer added to parent for JS/TS. Sonar threshold is 15 (most languages) / 25 (C family). Empirical study (JSS 2022) shows cognitive vs cyclomatic performance is 'extremely close' after controlling for size.

title: Six Human-Centric Readability Dimensions from CoReEval (Oct 2025) for Structured Code Review Prompts
summary: The CoReEval benchmark (arxiv:2510.16579, Oct 2025) evaluated 10 LLMs across 1.4M evaluations and derived six developer-validated readability dimensions for functional code: Code Structure, Nesting, Understandable Goal, Code Length, Inline Actions, Reading Flow. For unit tests: Test Structure, Test Names, Assertions, Test Code Size, Test Purpose Clarity, Fixture Simplicity. Using developer-guided prompts embedding these criteria improved aspect-coverage dramatically (e.g., assertions coverage 15% → 94%, structure mentions 18% → 90%). However, even with guided prompts, LLM-human Pearson correlation for Java was only r=0.25 vs static model r=0.31, and near-zero for Python/CUDA. Key implication: static analysis outperforms or matches LLMs for production code readability; LLMs only lead on test code. LLMs tend to surface-level features: naming, indentation, comments. For the MCP, these six dimensions define a concrete 'ReadabilityProfile' biomarker that could be computed from static signals (nesting depth, inline complexity, reading-flow proxies like early-return count).
evidence: From full page fetch: six named dimensions verified, Java Pearson r=0.25 (LLM) vs r=0.31 (static), Python r≈0.00 for LLMs. Developer-guided prompting raises aspect coverage from ~15-18% to 90-94%.

title: GNN-Based Readability: Sequential Logic, Comments, Selection Logic, and Nested Structure Are the Most Important Subgraph Features
summary: A 2025 Journal of Software paper (Wiley, DOI 10.1002/smr.70048) employs GNNs with SubgraphX explainability on simplified program graphs to explain code readability classification. The four most influential code characteristics for readable/unreadable classification are: (1) sequential logic (straight-line code), (2) presence of code comments, (3) selection logic (if/else branching), (4) nested structure depth. GNNs achieve state-of-the-art performance on readability classification. Importantly, the models fail to capture naming convention quality — they miss poor identifier names as a readability signal. This identifies a gap: the MCP should weight both 'absence of helpful comments' and 'poor identifier naming' as distinct biomarkers. The nesting structure finding reinforces that DeepNesting (already weighted at 1.2) is correct but the project may underweight comment absence.
evidence: Search result confirms: sequential logic, code comments, selection logic, nested structure are top-4 GNN subgraph features. GNN models noted to fail on naming conventions. Paper published in Journal of Software: Evolution and Process, 2025.

title: LLM Voting Ensemble (4 LLMs + 2 Tools, Majority ≥3) Boosts Code Smell F1 by 5-7 Points
summary: A January 2026 IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering paper (arxiv:2601.09873) systematically evaluates LLMs vs static tools for code smell detection. Key findings: LLMs outperform tools on structurally clear smells (Large Class F1=0.88 Llama-3.3, Long Method F1=0.87 GPT-5-mini, Data Class all LLMs ≥0.85). Tools outperform LLMs on complex/relational smells (Long Parameter List tool precision=1.00, Shotgun Surgery JSpIRIT F1=0.69 vs LLM max 0.63). Best ensemble strategy: 6-way majority vote (4 LLMs + 2 static tools, ≥3 votes) raises Large Class to F1=0.93, Long Method to F1=0.89, Dispersed Coupling to F1=0.80. The MCP already detects GodClass and LongMethod via static rules; adding an optional LLM-vote pathway when the MCP is called by Claude could improve detection precision especially for ambiguous cases, without replacing static analysis.
evidence: Full page fetch from arxiv:2601.09873 confirms F1 scores: Large Class ensemble F1=0.93 vs best individual 0.88; Long Method 0.89 vs 0.87; Intensive Coupling ensemble over-flags by 31%. Voting threshold of ≥3/6 recommended.

title: Cognitive Complexity Weight Calibration: Default 15 Threshold Shows Only Modest Advantage Over Cyclomatic
summary: Empirical validation studies (JSS 2022, ESEM 2020) show that cognitive complexity correlates with understandability and defects at a statistically significant level (93% of metrics significant across 3 open-source systems), but its predictive performance over models using only traditional measures is 'extremely close.' The main value of cognitive complexity is not superior predictive power but superior actionability: it directly maps to code refactoring targets (nesting, structural increments). For calibrating the MCP's ComplexMethod weight (currently 1.5), the implication is that the threshold selection matters more than the metric choice. SonarSource uses 15 as the actionable threshold for most languages. Functions scoring >25 are strongly flagged. Mapping this to the MCP's √count-based scoring: at weight=1.5 a single ComplexMethod with CC>25 produces a score deduction of 1.5×√1=1.5 points, which is arguably too aggressive for a single large but organized function. A threshold-gated weight (e.g., weight=1.0 for CC 15-24, weight=1.5 for CC≥25) would better match empirical evidence.
evidence: Sonar default threshold 15 (most langs), 25 (C/C++). Empirical paper (JSS 2022): 'performance of models using Cognitive Complexity is extremely close to performance of models using only traditional measures.' 93% of metrics statistically significant re defects from researchgate sources.

title: LLM Complexity Optimal Zone: Peak Reasoning at Intermediate CC (~10), Not Minimum
summary: A January 2026 arXiv study (2601.21894) analyzing code complexity and LLM reasoning across many models finds a non-monotonic relationship: both very simple AND very complex code underperform compared to mid-range. Qwen models peak around CC≈10. 'High structural complexity actively degrades performance' with near-perfect negative correlations at the extremes. Cyclomatic complexity is a better predictor than LLOC for reasoning difficulty. The implication for the MCP refactoring loop: the target should not always be to minimize complexity to 1, but to reach an optimal 'refactorability zone.' Functions trivially simple (CC=1, single expression) may have been over-extracted and are also harder for LLMs to reason about in context. The current MCP loop targets score ≥9.5 which pushes toward simplicity — but for LLM-driven refactoring, a 'too-simple' warning (e.g., over-extracted micro-methods) could prevent counter-productive fragmentation.
evidence: Full page fetch confirms: Qwen peak at CC≈10, non-monotonic relationship, 'near-perfect negative correlations' beyond threshold. CC outperforms LLOC as reasoning predictor. 83% of experiments show range-restricted fine-tuning outperforms diverse-complexity training.

title: Identifier Naming Quality: Measurable Biomarker That Accounts for ~70% of Codebase Content
summary: Identifiers account for approximately 70% of source code content and poor identifier names increase comprehension effort measurably. Entropy-based naming quality metrics (term entropy × context coverage) can predict fault-proneness. Descriptive compound identifiers improve comprehension by up to 19% per controlled studies. The MCP currently detects no naming-quality biomarker beyond what tree-sitter extracts. An 'IdentifierNamingSmell' biomarker — detecting single-letter variables outside loop scope, abbreviation-heavy names (regex on identifier token-to-word ratios), or single-char parameter names — is measurable statically, language-neutral, and directly correlated to both human and LLM comprehension. This would be a Tier A/B biomarker requiring no tree-sitter grammar changes: pattern matching on captured identifier nodes from any existing grammar.
evidence: Identifiers = ~70% of source content (multiple papers). Comprehension improvement up to 19% for descriptive compound names. Entropy-based quality measurable statically. GNN explainability paper (2025) notes current tools fail to detect naming issues — a clear gap.

title: Comment Absence as a Distinct Biomarker: Readability GNNs Show Comments Are Top-4 Feature
summary: GNN readability research (Wiley 2025) consistently identifies code comment presence as one of the top-4 features driving readability classification. The MCP currently captures SATD (self-admitted technical debt comments) but does not score comment absence on complex code. A 'CommentDebt' biomarker — measuring comment-to-complexity ratio: functions with CC>10 and zero comments — is straightforwardly computable. Research from ICPC 2025 on personalized readability identifies six human-centric dimensions including 'Understandable Goal', which is proxied by docstring/comment presence. For the MCP: any function with cognitive complexity >10 and no JSDoc/docstring/inline comment block could receive a CommentDebt smell with weight ~0.5-0.8. This is particularly valuable for Tier A languages where tree-sitter can distinguish comment nodes from code nodes.
evidence: GNN subgraph analysis confirms code comments are top-4 readability feature. CoReEval six dimensions include 'Understandable Goal' (comment-proxied). Comment absence on complex functions is a measurable static signal. SATD detection already exists in MCP — CommentDebt is the complement.

title: Token Reduction: Cognitive-Load-Aware Inference Framework Achieves 45% Token Reduction
summary: A 2026 arXiv paper (2507.00653) formalizes cognitive load as an LLM inference optimization framework with three components mapped from cognitive science: Intrinsic Load (task complexity), Extraneous Load (prompt inefficiency), and Germane Load (productive reasoning). Applying this framework achieves up to 45% token reduction on code generation benchmarks without accuracy loss. For the MCP refactoring loop, this suggests structuring the `followUpInstruction` output to minimize extraneous cognitive load: keep context to a single function, pre-state the target smell explicitly before code, and use numbered steps that minimize re-reading. A parallel finding from the refactoring LLM literature (arxiv:2511.21788): 'breaking complex transformations into atomic steps' and 'injecting one-shot exemplars' are the two highest-impact prompt structure changes for refactoring accuracy. The MCP already provides numbered steps and example skeletons — these are validated best practices.
evidence: arxiv:2507.00653: up to 45% token reduction via cognitive load framework on code generation. arxiv:2511.21788: atomic steps + one-shot exemplars are top-2 prompt structure improvements for refactoring accuracy. MCP already uses numbered steps — validating the existing approach.

title: Opus 4.8 is the current state-of-the-art for agentic coding — same price as 4.7, released 28 May 2026
summary: Claude Opus 4.8 (released May 28, 2026, API: claude-opus-4-8) scores 88.6% on SWE-bench Verified (vs 87.6% for Opus 4.7) and 69.2% on SWE-bench Pro (vs 64.3%). Pricing is unchanged from Opus 4.7: $5/M input, $25/M output. It is ~4x less likely than Opus 4.7 to let code flaws pass unremarked, which is directly valuable for a self-correcting refactoring loop. The CLAUDE.md already documents Opus 4.7 effort guidance — this guidance applies identically to 4.8. The project's CLAUDE.md should be updated to reference 4.8 as the current best model for the refactoring loop orchestrator.
evidence: SWE-bench Pro 69.2% vs 64.3% for Opus 4.7; 4x improvement in self-caught code flaws. Same $5/$25 per million tokens pricing. Released May 28 2026, 41 days after Opus 4.7.

title: xhigh is the correct starting effort for the refactoring loop orchestrator; low/medium suffice for subagents
summary: The Anthropic API effort docs (authoritative source) define five levels: low (~0.3x tokens), medium (~0.6x), high (1.0x, default), xhigh (for 30+ min agentic/coding, Opus 4.7 and 4.8 only), max (highest capability, all models). For the main orchestrator driving the health-score refactoring loop, xhigh is the recommended starting point. For sub-tasks that are pre-decomposed (file navigation, syntax checks, generating boilerplate), low or medium effort cuts token cost by 40-70%. The project's CLAUDE.md already documents xhigh guidance for Opus 4.7 — this should be extended to show effort-per-role in a multi-agent loop rather than a uniform level.
evidence: Official API docs: 'Start with xhigh for coding and agentic use cases'. Low effort uses ~0.3x baseline tokens. 40-60% pipeline cost reduction cited from real deployments. max_tokens recommended at 64k+ for xhigh/max on Opus 4.7/4.8.

title: Adaptive thinking + effort is the current API contract; budget_tokens is deprecated on Opus 4.6+ and rejected on Opus 4.7/4.8
summary: On Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.8, manual extended thinking (budget_tokens) is rejected with a 400 error. The only supported thinking mode is adaptive (thinking: {type: 'adaptive'}), controlled entirely by the effort parameter. This is a breaking change if the project's refactoring loop passes budget_tokens to newer models. The project's CLAUDE.md still references budget_tokens in its API tips section — this is now stale and will cause errors on claude-opus-4-8. Adaptive thinking also auto-enables interleaved thinking (between tool calls), which is the recommended mode for agentic workflows. On Opus 4.8/4.7, thinking.display defaults to 'omitted' (not 'summarized') so thinking blocks return empty unless explicitly set to 'summarized'.
evidence: API docs: 'On Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Opus 4.7, adaptive thinking is the only supported thinking mode. Manual thinking: {type: enabled, budget_tokens: N} is rejected with a 400 error.' CLAUDE.md API tips section still references budget_tokens as a current pattern.

title: Effort routing on a single model can replace multi-model routing, reducing infrastructure complexity by ~15-25%
summary: The traditional pattern (Haiku for simple tasks, Sonnet for medium, Opus for hard) can now be replaced with a single Sonnet or Opus model with varying effort levels. Effort routing costs ~60% of uniform high-effort on the same model and eliminates three separate API integrations. However, for the Healthy AI Code MCP use case, hybrid is still better: use Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5 per M tokens) for read-only smell detection passes, Sonnet 4.6 at medium effort for applying mechanical fixes, and Opus 4.8 at xhigh for orchestration and complex multi-file refactoring. The three-tier model routing approach with Haiku/Sonnet/Opus still delivers ~51% cost reduction vs uniform Opus when session token volumes are high.
evidence: AgentMarketCap: low=0.3x, medium=0.6x, high=1.0x, max=1.5x tokens baseline. Sonnet 4.6 at medium effort vs Opus at high: 79.6% vs 80.8% on SWE-bench Verified at ~60% of cost. Augment Code routing guide: 51% cost reduction ($0.98 vs $2.02 per session) in three-tier routing.

title: Sonnet 4.6 is viable for execution-phase refactoring; Opus 4.8 is needed only for orchestration and novel-complexity smells
summary: Sonnet 4.6 scores 79.6% on SWE-bench Verified (vs 80.8% for Opus 4.6, 88.6% for Opus 4.8). The 1.2-point Sonnet-to-Opus gap on SWE-bench is the smallest in Claude's history. For pre-decomposed refactoring tasks (extract method, early return, parameter object) with a detailed instruction already produced by the orchestrator, Sonnet 4.6 at medium effort delivers near-Opus quality at $3/$15 per M tokens vs $5/$25 for Opus. The gap widens for multi-file architectural refactoring (15-19 points on MCP Atlas). Practical split: Opus 4.8 at xhigh for the planning and health-score analysis phase; Sonnet 4.6 at medium for applying the numbered refactoring steps produced by code_health_auto_refactor.
evidence: Augment Code routing guide: Opus output tokens cost 67% more than Sonnet ($25 vs $15/MTok). Sonnet 4.6 handles multi-file code generation, standard refactoring, complex debugging. Opus reserved for multi-file refactoring, architecture decisions, orchestration.

title: Dynamic Workflows (Opus 4.8 feature) enables parallel subagent refactoring at scale — capped at 1000 subagents, 16 concurrent
summary: Claude Opus 4.8 ships Dynamic Workflows (research preview, Claude Code only, Enterprise/Team/Max plans). This lets Claude write orchestration scripts that spin up to 1000 subagents (16 concurrent) in a single session, with plan state stored in script variables — not the context window. For the Healthy AI Code MCP, this could enable analyzing and refactoring entire codebases in parallel: one subagent per file, all health scores computed simultaneously, then a ranked fix queue executed in parallel. Token cost stays bounded because only final results return to the orchestrator context. Limitation: Claude Code only in research preview; not available via raw API in May 2026.
evidence: Anthropic: 'handles codebase-scale migrations across hundreds of thousands of lines', 'capped at 16 concurrent and 1,000 total per run', 'plan lives in script variables, not Claude's context, so only the final answer returns to your session'. Available on Enterprise, Team, Max plans.

title: Code-health score can drive automated effort-level selection in the refactoring loop
summary: The Triage framework (arXiv:2604.07494, April 2026) proposes using code health signals to route tasks to model tiers. The core insight applies directly to this project: when a file already scores >=9.0 (HEALTHY_THRESHOLD), use Sonnet at low effort for the re-review pass. When score is 7.0-9.0, use Sonnet at medium effort for refactoring. When score <7.0 (approaching PROBLEMATIC_THRESHOLD), use Opus at xhigh. This avoids paying Opus-level tokens for files that are near-target. The project already computes scores and thresholds — adding effort routing based on current score is a one-line parameter addition per loop iteration.
evidence: Triage paper: CodeHealth composite score (25+ sub-factors) used to route to cheaper vs premium models. Clean, well-structured code can be modified correctly by cheaper models; messy/complex code requires frontier models. Thresholds enable automatic tier escalation.

title: Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5 per M tokens is the correct model for read-only health review passes in the loop
summary: Haiku 4.5 runs at 97 tokens/second and costs $1/$5 per M tokens — 3x cheaper on input and 5x cheaper on output vs Opus 4.8. For the read-only health review pass (calling code_health_review to check the current score before deciding whether to continue the loop), Haiku 4.5 at low effort is sufficient. The critical threshold check (score >= 9.5 → loopComplete: true) requires no deep reasoning, just reading the structured JSON response. Routing re-review passes to Haiku reduces per-iteration cost significantly when 3-6 iterations are typical.
evidence: Haiku 4.5: $1/$5/MTok, 97 tokens/sec. Routing re-review and lint-level checks to Haiku saves $0.52 per session in the Augment Code worked example. Augment Code: 'read-only tasks don't need the most capable model and can cost 5-10x less tokens.'

title: The 'max' effort level should be avoided for iterative refactoring — adds cost for marginal quality gain and can cause overthinking on structured outputs
summary: Anthropic's official docs explicitly warn: 'On most workloads max adds significant cost for relatively small quality gains, and on some structured-output or less intelligence-sensitive tasks it can lead to overthinking.' The refactoring loop produces structured outputs (numbered step instructions, target function names, predicted deltas) that are already well-defined by the tool schema. Using max effort on these passes wastes tokens on extra thinking that does not improve fix quality. The documented recommendation is xhigh as the practical ceiling for agentic coding; reserve max only for genuinely frontier problems like first-time analysis of completely novel code patterns.
evidence: API docs: 'Reserve [max] for genuinely frontier problems. On most workloads max adds significant cost for relatively small quality gains, and on some structured-output or less intelligence-sensitive tasks it can lead to overthinking.' CLAUDE.md already documents max effort for score<5 — this guidance is sound but should be tightened.

title: Interleaved thinking (automatic in adaptive mode) improves multi-step tool-call quality without additional configuration
summary: Adaptive thinking automatically enables interleaved thinking on Opus 4.6/4.7/4.8 and Sonnet 4.6. This means the model can reason between individual tool calls in the refactoring loop (review → auto-refactor → apply → re-review), rather than only at the start of the turn. For the Healthy AI Code MCP, this is directly beneficial: the model's per-tool-call reasoning is more coherent, reducing the chance of applying a fix that reverses a previous improvement. The CLAUDE.md already documents the beta header for interleaved thinking on Sonnet 4.6 — this is now automatic on adaptive mode and requires no header.
evidence: Adaptive thinking docs: 'Adaptive thinking also automatically enables interleaved thinking. This means Claude can think between tool calls, making it especially effective for agentic workflows.' No beta header required when using thinking: {type: 'adaptive'}.

title: SWE-bench pass-rate inflates correctness by ~6-11 percentage points: PatchDiff reveals
summary: An ICSE 2026 study found that 11% of SWE-bench 'solved' patches are actually incorrect. SWE-bench validates only against PR-modified test files, ignoring the rest of the repo's test suite. 7.8% of plausible patches fail when ALL developer tests are run. 29.6% of plausible patches show behavioral divergence when tested with LLM-generated differentiating tests (PatchDiff). 28.6% of behaviorally divergent patches are confirmed wrong by manual inspection. Resolution rates are inflated by 6.4 absolute percentage points. The PatchDiff technique generates differentiating tests using GPT-4o-mini with call-trace context, then filters flaky tests. If Healthy AI Code MCP claims a pass-rate metric (e.g., '92% of files reach score >= 9.5 after one loop'), the benchmark must run the FULL post-refactor test suite, not just a subset. Partial test suites produce inflated success numbers.
evidence: 7.8% fail full test suite, 29.6% behaviorally divergent, 6.4pp inflation in resolution rate, 82.7% of suspicious patches not caught by running all developer tests

title: SWE-Refactor: the first credible repository-level refactoring benchmark (1,099 Java instances, 3-stage validation)
summary: SWE-Refactor (arXiv 2602.03712, Feb 2026) comprises 1,099 developer-written behavior-preserving refactorings from 18 Java projects: 922 atomic (Extract Method 441, Move Method 410, Inline Method 71) and 177 compound. Validation uses 3 stages: (1) AST-based static analysis via RefactoringMiner + PurityChecker, (2) full test suite compilation and execution, (3) manual inspection of 200 random instances. RAG retrieval uses a separate non-overlapping oracle dataset. Top LLM results: DeepSeek-V3 41.58%, GPT-4o-mini 39.85%, open-source models under 1.1%. GPT-5.1-Codex drops from 82.6% on atomic to 39.4% on compound. This is a direct competitor benchmark and a template for how Healthy AI Code MCP should design its own public evaluation suite.
evidence: 1,099 instances, 3-stage validation pipeline, DeepSeek-V3 41.58% success, open-source models < 1.1%, 82.6% atomic vs 39.4% compound for best agent

title: Defects4J has 21.6% non-reproducible bugs: six workability requirements every APR benchmark must satisfy
summary: A 2025 study (arXiv 2604.26674) on Defects4J 2.0 found that 180 of 835 bugs (21.6%) are not workable under strict APR evaluation: 126 due to order-dependent test suites, 23 flaky tests, 26 compilation failures, 5 result mismatches. Removing trivially-fixable under-specified defects (59 cases, 9% of workable set) reduces jGenProg's reported fix-rate from 13.9% to 7.9%. Six workability requirements defined: parseable source, standard compiler invocation, executable test suite, per-test result reporting, per-test coverage collection, consistent cross-order test results. Since Healthy AI Code MCP already validates against Defects4J (Java calibration), it should adopt these six requirements as a published checklist for any benchmark dataset it releases.
evidence: 21.6% non-reproducible, 9% under-specified, fix-rate drops from 13.9% to 7.9% after exclusions, 6 concrete workability requirements defined

title: RefactoringMiner 3.0 achieves 99.7% F1 on Java refactoring detection: use it as oracle for transformer output verification
summary: RefactoringMiner 3.0 achieves Precision=99.8%, Recall=99.6%, F1=99.7% for statement-level mappings and detects 100+ refactoring types. For inter-file mappings: Precision/Recall=99.6% while all competing tools score recall=0%. RefactoringMiner++ extends this to C++ with perfect precision/recall on seeded benchmarks. When Healthy AI Code MCP evaluates whether its automated transformers (extract-method, early-return, parameter-object) are behavior-preserving, it should use RefactoringMiner as the oracle to confirm the correct refactoring type was applied and no unintended code changes occurred. This is the same approach SWE-Refactor uses. The project currently has no automated refactoring verification oracle -- this is a gap.
evidence: F1=99.7%, Precision=99.8%, Recall=99.6%, 100+ refactoring types, inter-file mappings 99.6% vs competitors at 0%

title: Benchmark Health Index: static fixture sets lose ranking signal in under 2 years; saturation affects even frontier models
summary: A 2026 meta-analysis (arXiv 2602.11674) of 106 benchmarks from 91 models defines three health axes: Discrimination Power (Gini coefficient), Anti-Saturation (headroom before ceiling effects), Impact. Static benchmarks have a median discriminative lifespan under 12,000 questions and lose signal in under 2 years. HumanEval is already saturated (Gemini 3.1 Pro 94.3%, Claude Opus 4.6 91.3%). EvoEval shows LLMs scoring high on standard benchmarks drop an average 39.4% on evolved variants. Healthy AI Code MCP's current fixture set (healthy/ and unhealthy/ directories) will saturate as LLMs are trained on public examples. Mitigation: rotate fixture sets quarterly, use procedurally generated fixtures, or release held-back test fixtures only for official leaderboard submissions.
evidence: static benchmarks lose signal in < 2 years, 39.4% average drop on evolved variants, HumanEval saturated above 88% for frontier models

title: HOW2BENCH 55-point checklist: rigor, reliability, reproducibility are the 2025 gold standard for credible benchmark construction
summary: A decade-scale survey of 572 code benchmarks (arXiv 2501.10711) introduces HOW2BENCH with 55 checklists around three principles: Rigor in construction (task selection, difficulty calibration, diversity), Reliability in evaluation (test coverage, oracle quality, reproducible results), Reproducibility in release (Docker environments, public artifacts, licensing). Key finding: in 2025 alone, benchmarks ignoring code coverage when providing test cases nearly matched the total count from the previous 10 years. Before publishing any public benchmark for Healthy AI Code MCP, HOW2BENCH checklist compliance should be reported alongside the benchmark data. This positions the project as methodologically rigorous in academic contexts.
evidence: 55 checklists, 572 benchmarks surveyed 2014-2025, 2025 benchmark count ignoring test coverage nearly matches entire prior decade

title: Iterative LLM refactoring converges in 2-3 iterations; lack of explicit stopping criteria causes over-refactoring and comment stripping
summary: A 2026 large-scale study (arXiv 2602.21833) of GPT-5.1 on 230 Java snippets across 5 iterations found: structural adjustments concentrate in the first 2 iterations (76% unchanged lines by v1->v2, 86% by v2->v3, 92% by v4->v5). LLMs remove inline comments almost completely. Naming-focused prompts cause oscillatory renaming. No explicit stopping criteria were tested. The current Healthy AI Code MCP claim of 'reaches 10.0 in 2-6 iterations' aligns with convergence findings, but needs publication of statistical significance data (median, IQR, p-values). The project should formally define stopping criteria (score >= 9.5 AND delta per iteration < 0.1) and warn operators about comment-stripping as a documented side effect of the loop.
evidence: 76% unchanged lines by iteration 2, 92% by iteration 5, near-complete inline comment removal, oscillatory renaming with naming-focused prompts

title: LLM benchmark contamination reaches 45% on some public datasets: public fixture files are a concrete leakage risk
summary: Studies in 2025 (LessLeak-Bench arXiv 2502.06215, AntiLeakBench ACL 2025) find contamination levels up to 45% in popular LLMs on widely-used benchmarks. LessLeak-Bench scanned 83 SE benchmarks and found widespread data leakage. OpenAI's Frontier Evals team found models can reproduce original benchmark problem statements verbatim from task IDs alone. Since fixture files in packages/core/tests/fixtures/ are in a public GitHub repo, any LLM trained after the repo's public date has potentially seen those fixtures. The project's self-reported benchmark numbers could reflect memorization rather than genuine refactoring capability. Mitigation: maintain a private held-out test set not in the public repo, and rotate fixtures after each major model generation.
evidence: contamination up to 45% detected in popular LLMs, 83 SE benchmarks found to have leakage, models reproduce problem statements verbatim from task IDs

title: SmellyCode++ (2025): 107,554 annotated Java samples for 4 smell types -- an external calibration dataset for biomarker precision/recall
summary: SmellyCode++ (Nature Scientific Data, 2025) is a multi-label dataset of 107,554 Java samples from 103 projects annotated for God Class, Data Class, Feature Envy, and Long Method. F1 scores achieved by best detectors: Data Class 95.89%, God Class 94.48%, Feature Envy 88.68%, Long Method 88.87%. A separate 2025 EASE study benchmarked GPT-4.0 vs DeepSeek-V3 on a cross-language dataset (Java, Python, JavaScript, C++) finding GPT-4.0 achieves 0.95 precision on Large Class but only 0.41 recall overall. These datasets can serve as external calibration gold standards for Healthy AI Code MCP's smell detection. The project's 28 biomarkers cover more smell types than these benchmarks evaluate -- an opportunity to publish the first multi-language, multi-smell precision/recall evaluation at scale.
evidence: 107,554 annotated samples, F1 > 88% for 4 smells, GPT-4.0 recall only 0.41 overall vs 0.95 precision on best smell type

title: GitHub MCP server offline evaluation: tool-selection F1 plus argument hallucination rate as two independent metrics
summary: GitHub's production evaluation of their GitHub MCP Server (GitHub Blog, May 2025) uses two metric families: (1) Tool Selection: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, plus confusion matrices. (2) Argument Quality: argument hallucination rate (invalid argument names), all-expected-args rate, all-required-args rate, exact value match rate. Ground truth is natural-language queries paired with expected tool calls and expected arguments. They acknowledge 'benchmark volume is the weak point'. For Healthy AI Code MCP: each of the 27 MCP tools should have offline test cases measuring whether the LLM calls the right tool and supplies correct arguments. This is a concrete evaluation gap absent from the project today.
evidence: Two independent metric families: tool selection (F1 + confusion matrix) + argument quality (hallucination rate, exact match rate)

title: CodeScene 2026 whitepaper: code health below threshold increases AI-assisted defect risk by 30% -- empirical external validation benchmark
summary: CodeScene's January 2026 peer-reviewed whitepaper found AI coding assistants increase defect risk by at least 30% in unhealthy code. The loveholidays case study shows unguarded agentic coding with Claude caused declining code health, reversed after code-health-aware safeguards. CodeScene also launched a competing CodeHealth MCP server. For Healthy AI Code MCP: the 30% defect increase claim provides a concrete benchmark anchor. The project should validate whether its own score thresholds (9.5 AI_READY, 9.0 HEALTHY) correlate with defect rates in the same direction. Current calibration is Java-only (Defects4J). Replicating this study with all 28 biomarkers on a broader multi-language dataset would establish scientific credibility and differentiate from CodeScene.
evidence: 30%+ defect risk increase in unhealthy code (peer-reviewed), CodeHealth MCP server launched as direct competitor, loveholidays case study

title: Mutation testing for refactoring correctness: mutant score before/after as an oracle-independent behavior-preservation check
summary: A 2025 Springer study introduced MeteoR, a mutation-testing tool for verifying test-code refactorings by comparing mutation scores and mutant behavior before and after transformation. Mutation score maintained post-refactoring confirms behavioral equivalence even when the existing test suite is under-specified (per the Defects4J findings). For Healthy AI Code MCP: after automated transformers (extract-method, early-return) are applied, running mutation testing on the before/after pair provides an oracle-independent behavior-preservation check stronger than just running the existing test suite. The project should add mutation score preservation as a secondary validity metric in its benchmark design.
evidence: MeteoR validates refactoring behavior via mutation score comparison; behavioral equivalence confirmed by unchanged mutant kill set before/after

title: CodeScene has already launched a directly competing CodeHealth MCP Server
summary: CodeScene shipped a CodeHealth MCP Server (currently in early access at $9/month) that exposes code-health analysis as MCP tools in a self-correcting refactoring loop — virtually identical in concept to Healthy AI Code MCP. It claims 90-100% fix rates with MCP-augmented data vs. ~20% without, runs fully locally, supports 30+ languages, and integrates with Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codeium. Pricing is €8/month per repo with a 30-day trial. It targets the AI_READY_THRESHOLD of 9.5/10 explicitly. This is the primary direct competitor and it has first-mover advantage in brand recognition (CodeScene has $11.8M raised, established enterprise contracts, and ISO 27001 certification).
evidence: CodeScene MCP page confirms: 'code_health_review', 'pre_commit_code_health_safeguard' tools, '25+ factors', 90-100% fix rate claim, €8/month pricing, runs fully locally, AGENTS.md workflow framework, AI-Ready threshold of 9.5.

title: Open-core model with community-free / enterprise-paid is the proven dev-tool GTM playbook
summary: HashiCorp (Terraform, Vault), Grafana, GitLab, and Supabase all follow the same pattern: open-source core to maximize adoption, proprietary enterprise features (SSO/SAML, audit logs, RBAC, portfolio dashboards, compliance reports) behind paid tiers. The key insight is that individual developers pay nothing but become internal champions who then sell the enterprise tier to their company. For Healthy AI Code MCP, the practical application is: keep all 28 biomarkers + scoring engine + MCP tools fully open-source on npm and GitHub, then build an enterprise layer gating: portfolio-level dashboards across repos, SBOM/compliance exports, goal-tracking SLA enforcement, team-level knowledge-loss reports, and CI/CD gate integrations. The per-active-author pricing model CodeScene uses ($9/mo per repo, or per-author for orgs) is directly applicable.
evidence: HashiCorp: open core + enterprise = acquisition by IBM for $6.4B. Grafana: SAML, audit logs, RBAC behind enterprise license. CodeScene: €18/author/month Standard vs free for open-source, enterprise = custom pricing + dedicated success manager. CodeRabbit: $60M Series B at $550M valuation in September 2025.

title: MCP Registry official listing + MCP Server Cards (.well-known) = primary discovery channel in 2026
summary: The official MCP Registry (governed by Agentic AI Foundation / Linux Foundation since Dec 2025) has 9,652 servers and is the primary discovery channel for MCP tools. The 2026 roadmap commits to 'MCP Server Cards' — a standard for exposing server metadata via .well-known URLs so crawlers and registries discover capabilities without direct connections. Healthy AI Code MCP should: (1) register in the official Agentic AI Foundation MCP registry immediately, (2) implement .well-known/mcp-server-card.json with detailed capability metadata, (3) list on Glama.ai (secondary registry with trust scores), and (4) publish on npm under @healthy-ai-code scope with keywords 'mcp code-health biomarkers tree-sitter refactoring' to capture the 97M/month SDK download channel. Claude Code's built-in MCP installer means discoverability via npm is directly tied to first-run experience.

title: Calibration data as a long-term moat: publish multi-language smell thresholds backed by real defect datasets
summary: The project already has empirical calibration for Java via Defects4J. title: PLG flywheel design: usage data from open-source users should inform calibration improvements
summary: Cursor built a data flywheel where accept/reject actions on code suggestions become training signals. title: Triple Debt Model: Technical + Cognitive + Intent Debt as a unified framework
summary: Storey et al. (March 2026, arXiv:2603.22106) formalise the Triple Debt Model. Technical debt lives in code, cognitive debt lives in people (erosion of shared understanding), and intent debt lives in artifacts (absence of explicit rationale, goals, and constraints). The paper argues that AI-accelerated codebases are accumulating all three simultaneously: AI writes clean-looking code fast, but that code carries no externalized rationale, and the team who accepted it understands it less than code they wrote themselves. The paper explicitly surfaces intent debt as the gap that blocks both human developers and AI agents from safely evolving a system — a direct fit for what Healthy AI Code MCP measures. No quantitative formulas are proposed; the paper is definitional and framing-oriented, not prescriptive. The authors call diagnostic methods 'future work'.
evidence: Paper title: 'From Technical Debt to Cognitive and Intent Debt: Rethinking Software Health in the Age of AI', arXiv:2603.22106, March 2026. Authors identify intent debt as 'the absence or erosion of explicit rationale, goals, and constraints that guide how humans and agents evolve the system' — directly naming AI agent safety as a motivation.

title: GenAI-Induced SATD (GIST): AI attribution markers as a new biomarker class
summary: An empirical study of 6,540 LLM-referencing source code comments (Python/JS, Nov 2022–Jul 2025) found 81 that also contain SATD markers (1.47% intersection rate). These 'GIST' comments fall into 4 roles: Catalyst (41.98%), Source (27.2%), Mitigator (23.46%), Neutral (7.4%). The shift relative to traditional SATD: test debt rises from 2% to 21%, requirement debt from 14% to 21%, design debt drops from 72% to 41%. The knowledge-deficit pattern — 'TODO: Copilot suggested this function (I have no clue what the regex is doing)' — is the most actionable signal for intent debt. Detection recipe: case-insensitive regex for (LLM|AI|GPT|ChatGPT|Copilot|Gemini|Claude) + (generated|suggested|written|created) + (TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX) within the same comment block. Cohen's κ = 0.896 for inter-annotator agreement confirms high reliability. This is directly implementable as a new 'AiAttributedSATD' biomarker with weight ~0.8-1.0 in the scoring formula.
evidence: Study: 'TODO: Fix the Mess Gemini Created', arXiv:2601.07786, Jan 2026. 81 confirmed GIST comments. Test debt 10x higher in AI-assisted code. Uncertainty phrases ('don't know', 'not sure', 'no clue') co-occurring with AI attribution are the primary signal of knowledge deficit. Detection uses two-filter approach with validated regex patterns.

title: Comprehension Debt: 4 accumulation patterns measurable via proxy signals in code
summary: A qualitative study of 207 students over 8 weeks (621 reflective diaries) identified 4 comprehension debt accumulation patterns: (1) AI-as-black-box acceptance, (2) context-mismatch debt (AI output is syntactically correct but misaligned with the surrounding design), (3) dependency-induced atrophy (developers stop acquiring understanding), (4) verification-bypass (deferred or absent testing of AI output). While the paper explicitly states CD cannot be detected by static analysis alone (it lives in team cognition), patterns 2 and 4 leave code-level traces: context-mismatch debt manifests as style inconsistency, naming drift, and architectural violations; verification-bypass manifests as functions with no corresponding test coverage and AI-attributed TODO+test debt. A controlled RCT with 52 engineers found AI-assisted developers scored 17% lower on comprehension quizzes despite equal task completion time. This validates that AI-assisted code carries hidden comprehension cost regardless of surface quality.
evidence: arXiv:2604.13277, 'Comprehension Debt in GenAI-Assisted Software Engineering Projects', 2026. RCT: 52 engineers, ~17% comprehension score reduction (50% vs 67% on follow-up quiz). Four patterns from 621 diary entries.

title: Code-comment inconsistency as a direct intent-debt biomarker — LLM-powered detection at scale
summary: Multiple ICSE 2025 papers and tools (RustC4, DocChecker, ICSE'25 paper) demonstrate that LLM-based code-comment inconsistency detection is now production-viable. DocChecker achieves 72.3% accuracy on ICCD (inconsistency code-comment detection) tasks, outperforming GPT-3.5 and CodeLlama. The approach: embed the function body and its comment independently, compute semantic distance — high distance signals a stale or misleading comment. This is directly implementable as a 'StaleComment' or 'CommentCodeDivergence' biomarker. For the existing MCP server's scoring model, this would require per-function embedding comparison (can be done offline, not in the hot path). A lighter heuristic: flag comments containing past-tense verbs or removed variable names that no longer exist in the function body. This specifically targets the intent-debt case where a comment once captured rationale but has drifted from the code it explains.
evidence: ICSE'25 paper: 'Code Comment Inconsistency Detection and Rectification Using a Large Language Model'. DocChecker: 72.3% accuracy on ICCD. RustC4: LLM + program analysis for Rust-specific constraints in comments (ASE'24).

title: SonarQube AI Code Assurance (2025): industry precedent for AI-code-specific quality gating
summary: SonarQube 2025.1 LTA shipped autodetect AI code — it identifies GitHub Copilot-generated code via user behavior patterns, badges it with 'Contains AI Code', and routes it through a stricter quality gate. The 2025.3 release added full Rust support including Cognitive Complexity and Cyclomatic Complexity metrics (85 rules). This establishes an industry precedent: code that was AI-generated should be held to a higher quality bar, not a lower one. For Healthy AI Code MCP, the actionable implication is: when AI-attribution signals (GIST patterns) are detected in a file, the AI_READY_THRESHOLD should be raised from 9.5 to a higher value (e.g., 9.7) for that file, or a mandatory 'AiAttributedSATD = 0' gate should be added. This creates a distinction between human-written code that scores 9.5 and AI-assisted code that scores 9.5 but carries unresolved knowledge-deficit comments.
evidence: SonarQube Server 2025.1 LTA release notes and 2025.2 AI autodetect documentation. AI Code Assurance feature launched 2025. Rust Cognitive Complexity added in 2025.3.

title: Epistemic debt / knowledge-deficit comment patterns: regex biomarker implementable today
summary: The 'epistemic debt' framing (failingfast.io, Feb 2026) and the GIST research converge on a practical set of regex-detectable signals in source code comments that indicate the developer lacked understanding when they accepted code. These are: (1) first-person uncertainty phrases: 'I don't know', 'not sure', 'no idea', 'unclear', 'I have no clue'; (2) deferred validation: 'TODO' + ('test', 'verify', 'validate', 'check', 'confirm') within 3 lines; (3) AI attribution + question markers: AI tool name + ('?', 'why', 'what does this', 'does this work'); (4) orphaned TODO comments older than N commits where the associated code has changed. Combined, these form a 'KnowledgeDeficitComment' biomarker. Weight suggestion: 0.8 (similar to existing KnowledgeLoss weight of 1.0). This complements the existing SATD detection the project already has — it adds the AI-specificity layer and the uncertainty-language layer which the current SATD detection likely lacks.
evidence: GIST study (arXiv:2601.07786): uncertainty language patterns identified and validated (κ=0.896). Epistemic debt framing from failingfast.io Feb 2026. Current project already has SATD detection but no AI-attribution or uncertainty-language overlay.

title: Thoughtworks Technology Radar v34 (April 2026): codebase cognitive debt as industry-level 'Adopt' signal
summary: Thoughtworks Technology Radar Volume 34 (April 2026) designates 'codebase cognitive debt' as a top-tier concern, warning that AI-driven change velocity combined with Coding Agent Swarms is creating a reinforcing loop: small changes cause unexpected failures, fixes cause regressions, and teams progressively lose the ability to guide AI. The Radar recommends three countermeasures: (1) feedback sensors for coding agents, (2) tracking team cognitive load, (3) architectural fitness functions. For a code health MCP server, 'architectural fitness functions' is the most actionable: these are automated assertions that key architectural invariants hold — similar to what the existing architecture debt analyzer does. The Radar's framing provides strong external validation that the cognitive/intent debt dimension is a genuine industry need, not an academic niche. evidence: ThoughtWorks Technology Radar vol. 34, April 2026. Press release: 'As AI Accelerates Software Complexity, Thoughtworks Technology Radar Urges a Return to Engineering Fundamentals to Combat Cognitive Debt'.

title: Documentation coverage as a first-class intent-debt metric: docstring absence rates by function type
summary: Tools like docstr-coverage (PyPI) and pydocstring-coverage already measure per-file and per-project docstring coverage percentages for Python. The missing piece for a code health tool is: (a) language-agnostic docstring/comment-header absence detection across the 46 supported languages, and (b) weighting by function visibility (public API functions lacking docs are more expensive than private helpers). Proposed biomarker: 'UndocumentedPublicAPI' — count of exported/public functions and classes with no leading doc comment or docstring, weighted by estimated call frequency (fan-in from architecture debt analysis). Weight suggestion: 0.6-0.8 per unit. The project already has NamingClarity analysis; combining that with documentation absence creates a 'IntentClarity' composite score. Important nuance from 2025 research: AI-generated documentation that matches 'high quality human patterns' can be falsely flagged — so a heuristic-only approach has precision trade-offs.
evidence: docstr-coverage PyPI package. Project already has NamingClarity; lacks documentation coverage as distinct biomarker. 2025 research note: AI-generated doc detection has precision issues (heuristic approach flagging high-quality human docs as AI-generated).

title: Orphaned/stale TODO automation: TDCLEANER model provides ML-based detection approach
summary: A dedicated model called TDCLEANER (arXiv:2108.05846) uses offline learning on (code change, TODO comment, commit message) triples to identify obsolete TODO comments — those that were never resolved and whose associated code has since changed enough to make the TODO meaningless or contradictory. The two-stage approach (offline learning + online prediction) is trainable on any git repository. For Healthy AI Code MCP which already has git history access (via analyzeFileWithHistory), this is actionable: flag TODO comments that have survived N commits where the surrounding function body has been changed without addressing the TODO. This 'OrphanedTODO' biomarker is distinct from the existing SATD detection (which detects presence of TODO/FIXME), it adds temporal staleness. Weight suggestion: 0.5-0.7. This complements MethodTemporalCoupling which already uses git history.
evidence: TDCLEANER paper (arXiv:2108.05846). Project already accesses git history for MethodTemporalCoupling. Extended by 2025 research on LLM-based comment inconsistency detection (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3663529.3664458).

title: MCP token reduction: dynamic tool discovery cuts schema-transmission overhead 30-60%
summary: A NewStack article (2025) and StackOne comparison (2025) establish that sending all 27 tool schemas at every turn is a major token overhead source. Dynamic tool discovery — starting with 2-3 meta-tools and retrieving specific schemas on demand — reduces schema-transmission tokens by 30-60%. For the refactoring loop specifically: the loop only needs code_health_review, code_health_auto_refactor, and potentially code_health_apply on each turn. The other 24 tools (architecture debt, bus factor, security audit, etc.) should only be loaded when requested. The Speakeasy blog reports 100x token reduction via dynamic toolsets. For a loop with 10 iterations x 27 tools x ~200 tokens/schema = 54,000 tokens saved per session if reduced to 3 tools per turn. Combined with the existing prompt caching and token-efficient-tools beta the project already uses, this could reduce loop cost by an additional 30-40%.
evidence: NewStack 2025: 'How to Reduce MCP Token Bloat'. StackOne comparison of 4 MCP token optimization approaches. Speakeasy blog: 100x reduction via dynamic toolsets. GitHub: token-optimizer-mcp (ooples/token-optimizer-mcp) achieves 95%+ reduction via caching + compression.

title: SARIF 2.1.0: Native output format for CI/CD ecosystem ingestion
summary: SARIF 2.1.0 (OASIS standard) is the universal interchange format accepted by GitHub Code Scanning, GitLab, SonarQube, AWS CodeCatalyst, Azure DevOps, and IDE extensions (VS Code SARIF Explorer, JetBrains). The project already has `formatAsSarif()` in the public API, but the critical gap is how richly that SARIF is populated. Key fields for first-class GitHub integration: `partialFingerprints.primaryLocationLineHash` for deduplication across runs; `properties.security-severity` (0.0-10.0 float) for security smells; `fixes[].artifactChanges` for machine-readable suggested patches; `rule.properties.precision` ('very-high'/'high'/'medium'/'low') for result ordering; and `taxonomies` for mapping smells to CWE/OWASP entries. A per-file health score can be embedded as `run.properties.healthScore: 9.5` in the properties bag — SARIF's extensibility point. GitHub Code Scanning changed in July 2025: multiple SARIF runs with the same tool/category in the same file are no longer combined — each file must represent a single run. Maximum gzip-compressed upload size is 10 MB; 25,000 results per run (top 5,000 displayed by severity).
evidence: Project has `formatAsSarif()` but no evidence of partialFingerprints, fix objects, taxonomy mappings, or numeric health score embedded in properties bag. GitHub July 2025 change requires one run per file.

title: GitHub native Code Quality (public preview Oct 2025) — SARIF is the integration path
summary: GitHub launched 'Code Quality' in public preview in October 2025 and added an org-level dashboard in February 2026 and a Repository Enablement API in May 2026. It uses CodeQL to generate reliability and maintainability scores per repository (4-tier rating: Excellent / Good / Fair / Needs Improvement based on Error/Warning/Note severity). Third-party tools integrate via the same SARIF upload mechanism as Code Scanning — `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4` with `security-events: write` permission. If the project emits well-formed SARIF with correct severity levels, its smell findings will appear in the GitHub Code Quality dashboard alongside CodeQL findings. This is the highest-leverage distribution channel available today: every GitHub enterprise user who enables Code Quality becomes a potential user of the project's output without any SDK adoption step.
evidence: GitHub Code Quality public preview launched Oct 2025, org dashboard Feb 2026, Repository Enablement API May 2026. Third-party SARIF uploads integrate directly. Project's existing formatAsSarif needs severity mapping to align with GitHub's Excellent/Good/Fair/Needs-Improvement tiers.

title: GitLab Code Quality JSON format — lightweight second integration target
summary: GitLab Code Quality (gl-code-quality-report.json) accepts a JSON array with 6 fields: `description` (string), `check_name` (string), `fingerprint` (string, used as deduplication key — identical fingerprints collapse to single MR widget entry), `location.path` (string, repo-relative), `location.lines.begin` (int), and `severity` (enum: info / minor / major / critical / blocker). This is a much simpler schema than SARIF. Note: CodeClimate-based scanning was deprecated in GitLab 17.3 (2024) and is slated for removal in 19.0; GitLab now recommends direct SARIF uploads via the `codequality` artifact type. Adding a `code_health_review --format gitlab-json` output mode would give every GitLab CI user instant MR-integrated feedback without any external tooling. The fingerprint should be derived from: `md5(file + smell_type + start_line)` to be stable across runs.
evidence: Exact schema: description, check_name, fingerprint, location.path, location.lines.begin, severity (info/minor/major/critical/blocker). CodeClimate-based scanning deprecated GitLab 17.3; SARIF is now the preferred path. Project has no GitLab output format documented.

title: OpenSSF Scorecard SARIF output — emit compatible output to slot into Scorecard-style dashboards
summary: OpenSSF Scorecard (ossf/scorecard-action) already produces SARIF output and uploads it to GitHub Code Scanning. It has a SAST check that detects whether a project runs static analysis. If the project publishes a GitHub Action wrapper that runs code_health_review and uploads SARIF results, it satisfies Scorecard's SAST check (check #14), incrementing that check's score from 0 to potentially 10. Scorecard itself has 20 checks (0-10 scale each), weekly BigQuery dataset of 1M+ OSS projects, and a REST API at scorecard.dev. Scorecard does NOT have code-quality checks (cyclomatic complexity, maintainability) — it is security/supply-chain focused. The project should publish a GitHub Action that: (1) runs code_health_review, (2) uploads SARIF to Code Scanning, (3) fails CI if score < threshold. This Action would cause the host repo to pass Scorecard's SAST check automatically.
evidence: Scorecard SARIF output is confirmed; SAST check awards points for running any static analysis that uploads SARIF. Scorecard has no code quality/complexity metrics — complementary, not competing. ossf/scorecard-action auto-uploads SARIF.

title: SARIF taxonomy mappings to CWE/OWASP — elevate security smells to standard identifiers
summary: SARIF 2.1 `taxonomies` allows mapping results to external classification systems. The sarif-standard/taxonomies repo provides ready-made SARIF taxonomy files for CWE Top 25, OWASP Top 10, OWASP ASVS v4.0.2, OWASP Mobile Top 10, and NIST SP800-53. The project's security smells (SqlInjectionRisk → CWE-89, XssRisk → CWE-79, CommandInjectionRisk → CWE-78, HardcodedCredential → CWE-798, HardcodedApiKey → CWE-312) map directly to CWE entries. Embedding these taxonomy references in SARIF output means findings appear with standard CWE IDs in GitHub Code Scanning's filter UI and can be consumed by SCA/DAST tools that understand CWE. This is a one-time engineering investment (write the taxonomy reference map) with permanent interop benefit across every tool that ingests SARIF. Rule-level OWASP tags can also be added as `rule.properties.tags: ['owasp-top-10-a03:2021']`.
evidence: sarif-standard/taxonomies has ready-made taxonomy SARIF files. The project's security smells have clear CWE equivalents. GitHub Code Scanning UI filters by CWE when taxonomies are present. Project's existing formatAsSarif has no taxonomy mapping documented.

title: SARIF `fix` objects — encode smell-specific refactoring steps as machine-readable patches
summary: SARIF 2.1 `fixes[]` allows embedding suggested code changes directly in the result: each `fix` contains `artifactChanges[]` with `replacements[]` specifying `deletedRegion` and `insertedContent`. Tools like GitHub Copilot Autofix and Veracode Fix already consume SARIF `fix` objects to propose one-click patches. The project currently returns refactoring instructions as structured natural-language steps in `followUpInstruction`. Adding a `fix` object to SARIF output for mechanical smells (early-return for DeepNesting, extract-method for ComplexMethod) would let any SARIF-aware IDE (VS Code with SARIF Explorer, JetBrains) show inline quick-fix buttons, bypassing the need for an AI to interpret and apply the instructions. For smells that already have working AST transformers (TS/JS/PHP), the exact text replacement can be computed deterministically.
evidence: SARIF 2.1 spec defines fixes[].artifactChanges[].replacements[]. GitHub Copilot Autofix and Veracode Fix ingest SARIF fix objects. Project has AST transformers for TS/JS/PHP that compute exact replacements — these can populate fix objects for those 3 languages.

title: in-toto SCAI predicate — attest health score as supply chain attribute for SLSA pipelines
summary: The SCAI (Supply Chain Attribute Integrity) in-toto predicate (`https://in-toto.io/attestation/scai/v0.3`) allows tools to assert arbitrary named attributes about a source artifact. While designed for functional attributes (compiler flags, security features), the spec explicitly states 'the semantics of attribute and conditions fields are up to the producer and consumer.' A code quality tool can emit a SCAI attestation like: `{ attribute: 'HEALTHY_AI_CODE_SCORE', conditions: { score: 9.5, threshold: 9.0, passed: true }, evidence: { name: 'health-report.json' } }`. Combined with in-toto's test-result predicate (result: PASSED/WARNED/FAILED) and SLSA Source Track v1.2's quality gate integration, this creates a verifiable, cryptographically-signed audit trail of code health checks. SLSA v1.2 (in active development) allows custom `ORG_SOURCE_` prefixed levels. Organizations requiring SLSA compliance would gain a way to enforce code health as a build gate, not just a developer hint.
evidence: SCAI v0.3 predicate has open-ended attribute semantics. in-toto test-result predicate supports PASSED/WARNED/FAILED + passedTests/failedTests lists. SLSA Source v1.2 (active dev) has quality gate integration hooks. No existing competitor implements this for code health.

title: llms.txt / llms-full.txt — reduce AI assistant token overhead when consuming MCP documentation
summary: The llms.txt spec (proposed 2024, widely adopted by 2026 with 85% of developers using AI tools) defines a Markdown-format file at the project root or website root that AI coding assistants use to understand a project's API without parsing HTML. `llms.txt` contains a compact index with external links; `llms-full.txt` embeds all content for tools with large context windows. For this project, publishing both variants would reduce the token cost when Claude Code (or Cursor, GitHub Copilot) reads the MCP tool documentation before calling tools. Concretely: an llms-full.txt containing all 27 tool schemas, scoring formula, smell definitions, and threshold constants (~20-30KB) would replace multi-step file reads during session initialization. Anthropic specifically requested llms.txt for their own documentation; it is included in Google's A2A protocol. The AGENTS.md convention serves the in-repository equivalent use-case (agent-directed context).
evidence: llms.txt adopted by Anthropic's own docs on Mintlify; included in Google A2A protocol. llms-full.txt embeds all content for within-context-window APIs. Project's CLAUDE.md is a partial implementation but not a spec-compliant llms.txt served at a URL.

title: Roam competitor already exports SARIF from MCP — competitive pressure to match
summary: Roam (roam-code.com) is a direct competitor: local SQLite code graph, 28 languages, 57-227 MCP tools, health score 0-100, and SARIF 2.1.0 export on every applicable command via `--sarif` flag. It integrates with GitHub Code Scanning and GitLab CI. Its 0-100 scale (vs this project's 1-10) may appear more granular to users. Key differentiators this project has: richer smell taxonomy (28 biomarkers vs Roam's 24 detectors), temporal/behavioral analytics (hotspots, churn, bus factor), self-correcting refactoring loop with structured AI instructions, and calibrated thresholds (AI_READY=9.5). title: CycloneDX 1.7 formulation + quality annotations — embed health scores in SBOM for supply chain consumers
summary: CycloneDX 1.7 (released October 2025, ECMA-424 ratified) added Citations (verifiable data provenance) and expanded Formulations scope. The `formulation` field in a CycloneDX BOM can describe how components were produced, including test results and quality gates. The `annotations` object (CycloneDX 1.7) allows arbitrary annotators to attach signed claims to BOM elements. A code health MCP server could emit a CycloneDX annotation attaching a health score and smell summary to the component being analyzed, signed with the tool's key. This would let software composition analysis (SCA) tools (Dependency-Track, FOSSA, Snyk) show code health data alongside dependency/vulnerability data in a single BOM view. CycloneDX's ML-BOM profile is particularly relevant for AI-generated code: attaching health scores to AI-generated components creates an audit trail for AI code quality governance.
